```{python}
#| label: setup
import base64, io
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle, Polygon, FancyBboxPatch
from IPython.display import display, HTML, Markdown
from scipy.signal import correlate2d
from sklearn.datasets import load_sample_image

BLUE, ORANGE, GREEN, GREY, RED, INK = "#1f4fd8", "#E8833A", "#1a7f37", "#888888", "#b5302a", "#222222"
FILL = {"in": "#dfe8ff", "hid": "#FDE3C8", "out": "#dcf3e2", "grey": "#eeeeee"}
plt.rcParams.update({"mathtext.fontset": "cm", "font.size": 13, "axes.edgecolor": "#999999",
                     "xtick.color": "#555555", "ytick.color": "#555555"})

R = np.load("cnn_fa26_assets/results.npz")   # made by cnn_fa26_assets/make_results.py


def md(s):
    display(Markdown(s))


def n(x, d=3):
    """Format a number: trailing zeros off, and no negative zero."""
    s = f"{x:.{d}f}"
    s = s.rstrip("0").rstrip(".") if "." in s else s
    return "0" if s in ("-0", "") else s


def c(x):
    """A whole number with thousands separators."""
    return f"{int(x):,}"


def png_uri(fig):
    b = io.BytesIO()
    fig.savefig(b, format="png", dpi=150, facecolor="white")
    plt.close(fig)
    return "data:image/png;base64," + base64.b64encode(b.getvalue()).decode()


def show_fig(fig):
    display(HTML(f'<img src="{png_uri(fig)}">'))


def stack(figs):
    """Layer figures on top of each other; each click reveals the next one."""
    imgs = [f'<img src="{png_uri(figs[0])}">']
    imgs += [f'<img class="fragment" data-fragment-index="{i}" src="{png_uri(f)}">' for i, f in enumerate(figs[1:], 1)]
    display(HTML('<div class="r-stack">' + "".join(imgs) + "</div>"))


def steps(lines):
    """Each line appears on its own click. Line 0 is always visible."""
    out = [lines[0]]
    out += [f'::: {{.fragment fragment-index="{i}"}}\n{l}\n:::' for i, l in enumerate(lines[1:], 1)]
    md("\n\n".join(out))


def table(header, rows):
    s = "| " + " | ".join(header) + " |\n|" + ":---:|" * len(header) + "\n"
    s += "\n".join("| " + " | ".join(str(x) for x in r) + " |" for r in rows)
    md(s)


def conv(x, w, b=0, mode="valid"):
    """The sliding sum, with no flip of the filter (what deep learning libraries compute)."""
    return b + correlate2d(np.asarray(x, float), np.asarray(w, float), mode=mode)


def relu(z):
    return np.maximum(0, z)


def pool(a, s=2):
    h, w = a.shape[0] // s, a.shape[1] // s
    return a[:h * s, :w * s].reshape(h, s, w, s).max(axis=(1, 3))


def out_size(n_, f, p=0, s=1):
    return (n_ - f + 2 * p) // s + 1


def conv_params(f, c_in, k, bias=True):
    return (f * f * c_in + (1 if bias else 0)) * k


def fc_params(m, k):
    return (m + 1) * k


# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# Drawing helpers. Grids have their top-left corner at (x, y), one unit per cell.
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
def canvas(size, xlim, ylim):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=size)
    ax.set_xlim(*xlim)
    ax.set_ylim(*ylim)
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.axis("off")
    fig.subplots_adjust(0, 0, 1, 1)
    return fig, ax


def cells(ax, A, x=0, y=0, cmap=None, vmin=None, vmax=None, fs=15, text=True, face="white", title=None, tfs=14, fmt=None, lw=1.0):
    A = np.asarray(A, float)
    cm = plt.get_cmap(cmap) if cmap else None
    vmin = A.min() if vmin is None else vmin
    vmax = A.max() if vmax is None else vmax
    for r in range(A.shape[0]):
        for k in range(A.shape[1]):
            fc, tc = face, INK
            if cm:
                t = 0.5 if vmax == vmin else (A[r, k] - vmin) / (vmax - vmin)
                fc = cm(t)
                tc = "white" if 0.299 * fc[0] + 0.587 * fc[1] + 0.114 * fc[2] < 0.55 else INK
            ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x + k, y - r - 1), 1, 1, fc=fc, ec="#999999", lw=lw, zorder=2))
            if text:
                label = fmt(A[r, k]) if fmt else n(A[r, k])
                ax.text(x + k + 0.5, y - r - 0.5, label, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=fs, color=tc, zorder=3)
    if title:
        ax.text(x + A.shape[1] / 2, y + 0.35, title, ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=tfs, fontweight="bold", color="#444444", linespacing=1.3)


def frame(ax, x, y, h, w, color=ORANGE, lw=4):
    """Highlight the block of h rows and w columns whose top-left corner is at (x, y)."""
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x, y - h), w, h, fc="none", ec=color, lw=lw, zorder=5))


def arrow(ax, x0, y0, x1, y1, color="#777777", lw=1.6, style="-|>", z=4):
    ax.annotate("", xy=(x1, y1), xytext=(x0, y0), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle=style, color=color, lw=lw, shrinkA=0, shrinkB=0), zorder=z)


def block(ax, x, y, w, h, d, fc="#dfe8ff", ec=BLUE, lw=1.5, z=3, ox=0.55, oy=0.4):
    """A 3D box. Its front face has bottom-left corner (x, y); d is drawn up and to the right."""
    dx, dy = d * ox, d * oy
    ax.add_patch(Polygon([(x, y + h), (x + dx, y + h + dy), (x + w + dx, y + h + dy), (x + w, y + h)], fc=fc, ec=ec, lw=lw, zorder=z, alpha=0.85))
    ax.add_patch(Polygon([(x + w, y), (x + w + dx, y + dy), (x + w + dx, y + h + dy), (x + w, y + h)], fc=fc, ec=ec, lw=lw, zorder=z, alpha=0.6))
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x, y), w, h, fc=fc, ec=ec, lw=lw, zorder=z + 0.1))


def activation_icon(ax, x, y, width, height, color, lw=2.2):
    t = np.linspace(-1, 1, 60)
    shape = np.where(t < 0, -0.75, -0.75 + 1.75 * t)
    ax.plot(x + t * width / 2, y + shape * height / 2, color=color, lw=lw, solid_capstyle="round", zorder=7)


# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# Data used throughout: a real MNIST digit and two real photos
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
digit = R["sample_digit"]
digits = R["mnist_examples"]
order = R["shuffle_order"]
china = load_sample_image("china.jpg")[::2, ::2].mean(axis=2) / 255.0
flower = load_sample_image("flower.jpg")[::2, ::2] / 255.0

V_EDGE = np.array([[-1, 0, 1]] * 3)
H_EDGE = V_EDGE.T
BLUR = np.ones((3, 3)) / 9
SHARPEN = np.array([[0, -1, 0], [-1, 5, -1], [0, -1, 0]])
OUTLINE = np.array([[-1, -1, -1], [-1, 8, -1], [-1, -1, -1]])


def shifted(a, dx=0, dy=0):
    """Move an image; pixels moved in from outside are 0."""
    out = np.zeros_like(a)
    h, w = a.shape
    out[max(dy, 0):h + min(dy, 0), max(dx, 0):w + min(dx, 0)] = a[max(-dy, 0):h + min(-dy, 0), max(-dx, 0):w + min(-dx, 0)]
    return out
```

## Where We Are

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
**What we already know**

-   Every node does two steps: it **adds** its weighted inputs, then applies an **activation function**.
-   A layer of $k$ nodes after a layer of $m$ nodes has $(m + 1) \times k$ parameters.
-   The framework: choose $f(x, w)$, define a loss, find $w$ by gradient descent.
-   Deep learning deck: a **convolutional** network won ImageNet in 2012 and changed the field.
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
**Today's plan**

-   **Part 1.** Why regular networks struggle with images
-   **Part 2.** The 2D convolution: one filter on a grayscale image
-   **Part 3.** From 2D to 3D: color, stacks of filters, video and scans
-   **Part 4.** A whole CNN, with every number counted
-   **Part 5.** Why it works so well on images: four experiments
-   **Part 6.** How CNNs changed the field
:::
::::

::: {.key}
**The main message:** a CNN uses the same nodes as before, with two extra rules. Each node looks at a **small patch**, and all nodes **share the same weights**. Those two rules fit how images work.
:::

# Part 1. Why Not Use a Regular Network?

## An Image Is a Grid of Numbers

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12.6, 5.6), gridspec_kw=dict(width_ratios=[1, 1.02]))
ax[0].imshow(digit, cmap="gray", vmin=0, vmax=1)
r0, c0, size = 5, 8, 10
ax[0].add_patch(Rectangle((c0 - 0.5, r0 - 0.5), size, size, fc="none", ec=ORANGE, lw=3))
ax[0].set_title("A real MNIST digit: 28 × 28 pixels", fontsize=15, fontweight="bold", color="#444444")
ax[0].axis("off")
ax[1].set_xlim(-0.2, size + 0.2)
ax[1].set_ylim(-size - 0.2, 0.2)
ax[1].set_aspect("equal")
ax[1].axis("off")
cells(ax[1], digit[r0:r0 + size, c0:c0 + size], cmap="gray", vmin=0, vmax=1, fs=12.5, fmt=lambda v: f"{v:.1f}".replace("0.0", "0").replace("1.0", "1"))
ax[1].set_title("The orange box, as the computer sees it", fontsize=15, fontweight="bold", color="#444444")
fig.tight_layout()
show_fig(fig)
```

Each pixel is one number, from 0 (black) to 1 (white). A grayscale image is a **2D array**: rows and columns of numbers. Those numbers are our inputs $x_1, x_2, \dots$

## First Try: Flatten It and Use a Regular Network

```{python}
assert fc_params(784, 128) == 100480 and fc_params(150528, 1000) == 150529000 and fc_params(3000000, 1000) == 3000001000
```

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
```{python}
fig, ax = canvas((6.9, 5.3), (-0.6, 15.4), (-6.6, 5.7))
small = digit[4:24:2, 4:24:2]
cells(ax, small, x=-0.2, y=3.8, cmap="gray", vmin=0, vmax=1, text=False, lw=0.5)
ax.text(4.8, 4.4, "28 × 28 image", ha="center", fontsize=14, fontweight="bold", color="#444444")
arrow(ax, 10.0, -1.2, 11.0, -1.2)
xs = np.linspace(4.9, -5.2, 9)
for i, yy in enumerate(xs):
    if i in (4,):
        ax.text(11.6, yy, "⋮", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=17, color=INK)
        continue
    ax.add_patch(plt.Circle((11.6, yy), 0.42, fc=FILL["in"], ec=BLUE, lw=1.3, zorder=4))
    for j, y2 in enumerate(np.linspace(3.7, -4.0, 5)):
        ax.plot([11.6, 14.5], [yy, y2], color="#cccccc", lw=0.6, zorder=1)
for y2 in np.linspace(3.7, -4.0, 5):
    ax.add_patch(plt.Circle((14.5, y2), 0.42, fc=FILL["hid"], ec=ORANGE, lw=1.3, zorder=4))
ax.text(11.6, -6.15, "784 inputs", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=13)
ax.text(14.6, -6.15, "128", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=13)
show_fig(fig)
```
:::

::: {.column width="54%"}
Stack the rows into one long list and use it as the input layer. It works for small images, but the cost grows quickly.

**Problem 1: too many parameters.** Using $(m + 1) \times k$ for the **first layer alone**:

```{python}
table(["Image", "Inputs $m$", "Nodes $k$", "Parameters"], [
    ["28 × 28, gray", "784", "128", c(fc_params(784, 128))],
    ["224 × 224, color", "150,528", "1,000", c(fc_params(150528, 1000))],
    ["1000 × 1000, color", "3,000,000", "1,000", c(fc_params(3000000, 1000))],
])
```

A color image has 3 numbers per pixel, so $224 \times 224 \times 3 = 150{,}528$ inputs. More parameters need more data and memory, and they overfit more easily.
:::
::::

## Problem 2: Flattening Throws Away the Map

::: {.h360}
```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 6, figsize=(10.2, 3.95))
for j in range(6):
    ax[0, j].imshow(digits[j], cmap="gray", vmin=0, vmax=1)
    ax[1, j].imshow(digits[j].ravel()[order].reshape(28, 28), cmap="gray", vmin=0, vmax=1)
    ax[0, j].axis("off")
    ax[1, j].axis("off")
fig.text(0.5, 0.955, "Real digits", ha="center", fontsize=15, fontweight="bold", color="#444444")
fig.text(0.5, 0.475, "The same digits, with the pixels moved around in one fixed random order", ha="center", fontsize=15, fontweight="bold", color="#444444")
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.02, right=0.98, top=0.94, bottom=0.01, hspace=0.3, wspace=0.05)
show_fig(fig)
```
:::

-   You cannot read the bottom row. A fully connected network has no such trouble: it has no idea which inputs are neighbors.
-   Reorder the inputs and the weights can simply be reordered to match, so nothing is lost. We test this claim on real data in Part 5.

::: {.key}
A fully connected network treats a picture like a spreadsheet of unrelated columns. It ignores the most useful fact about images: **nearby pixels belong together**.
:::

## Problem 3: Same Digit, Different Inputs

```{python}
moved = shifted(digit, dx=2)
lit, lit2 = digit > 0.5, moved > 0.5
stay = (lit & lit2).sum() / lit.sum()
overlay = np.dstack([1 - lit2 * 0.25 - lit * 0.85, 1 - lit * 0.55 - lit2 * 0.55, 1 - lit * 0.15 - lit2 * 0.85]).clip(0, 1)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(11.6, 4.1))
for a, img, t in [(ax[0], digit, "A digit"), (ax[1], moved, "Moved 2 pixels right")]:
    a.imshow(img, cmap="gray", vmin=0, vmax=1)
    a.set_title(t, fontsize=15, fontweight="bold", color="#444444")
    a.axis("off")
ax[2].imshow(overlay)
ax[2].set_title("Pixels that are bright in each", fontsize=15, fontweight="bold", color="#444444")
ax[2].axis("off")
fig.tight_layout()
show_fig(fig)
```

```{python}
md(f"-   To us, these are the same 3. To a fully connected network, they are very different inputs: only **{stay:.0%}** of the bright pixels stay bright. (In the right panel, blue is the digit, orange is the moved copy, and dark is where they agree.)\n"
   "-   A weight is tied to one position. A network that learned a curve in one spot must learn it **again** for every other spot.")
```

## Three Facts About Images, Three Design Choices

| What we know about images | So we design the network to... | Name |
|:------------------:|:-----------------------:|:------:|
| **Locality:** a pixel relates most to its neighbors | Let each node see only a small patch | Local connections |
| **Repetition:** an edge looks the same anywhere in the image | Reuse the same weights at every position | Weight sharing |
| **Hierarchy:** edges form shapes, shapes form parts, parts form objects | Stack layers, and shrink the image along the way | Deep layers and pooling |

::: {.key}
A convolutional neural network (**CNN**) is what you get when you build these three facts into the network. We start with the smallest piece: one filter on a grayscale image.
:::

# Part 2. The 2D Convolution

## The Idea: A Small Filter That Slides

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="44%"}
A **filter** (or **kernel**) is a small grid of weights. It works like a stencil you slide across the image:

1.  Place the filter on a patch of the image.
2.  Multiply each pixel by the weight on top of it.
3.  Add the results. That one number goes in the output.
4.  Move the filter over one pixel and repeat.

The grid of outputs is called a **feature map**. It shows **where** in the image the filter found its pattern.
:::

::: {.column width="56%"}
```{python}
fig, ax = canvas((8.2, 4.8), (-0.3, 17.2), (-8.6, 1.4))
img = np.array([[0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1]] * 6)
cells(ax, img, cmap="gray", vmin=0, vmax=1, title="Image: 6 × 6")
for col, colr, ls in [(0, ORANGE, "-"), (1, ORANGE, ":"), (2, ORANGE, ":")]:
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((col, -3), 3, 3, fc="none", ec=colr, lw=3.4 if col == 0 else 1.8, ls=ls, zorder=5))
arrow(ax, 0.3, -6.7, 5.6, -6.7, color=ORANGE, lw=2.6)
ax.text(3, -7.25, "the filter moves right, then down", ha="center", va="top", fontsize=13.5, color="#444444")
cells(ax, V_EDGE, x=8.6, y=-1.5, cmap="RdBu", vmin=-2.4, vmax=2.4, fs=16, title="Filter: 3 × 3")
ax.text(10.1, -5.0, "our weights", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=13.5, color="#444444")
out = conv(img, V_EDGE)
cells(ax, out, x=13, y=-1, cmap="Oranges", vmin=0, vmax=5, fs=16, title="Feature map: 4 × 4")
arrow(ax, 6.3, -3, 8.3, -3)
arrow(ax, 11.9, -3, 12.8, -3)
show_fig(fig)
```
:::
::::

::: {.key}
A convolution is the same multiply-and-add from every node we have built. What is new is that it **repeats at every position** with the same weights.
:::

## Worked Example: Slide the Filter

```{python}
img = np.array([[0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1]] * 6)
OUT = conv(img, V_EDGE)
assert OUT.shape == (4, 4) and (OUT == np.array([[0, 3, 3, 0]] * 4)).all()


def term(w, x):
    return f"({w})({x})"


def slide_fig(pos, done):
    """pos: (row, col) of the filter, or None. done: how many outputs are filled in."""
    fig, ax = canvas((13.0, 6.6), (-0.3, 20.2), (-10.4, 0.95))
    cells(ax, img, cmap="gray", vmin=0, vmax=1, fs=17, title="Image")
    cells(ax, V_EDGE, x=8, y=-1.5, cmap="RdBu", vmin=-2.4, vmax=2.4, fs=18, title="Filter (weights)")
    shown = np.full(OUT.shape, np.nan)
    for i in range(done):
        shown[i // 4, i % 4] = OUT[i // 4, i % 4]
    for r in range(4):
        for k in range(4):
            v = shown[r, k]
            ax.add_patch(Rectangle((14 + k, -1 - r - 1), 1, 1, fc="white" if np.isnan(v) else plt.get_cmap("Oranges")(v / 5), ec="#999999", zorder=2))
            if not np.isnan(v):
                ax.text(14.5 + k, -1 - r - 0.5, n(v), ha="center", va="center", fontsize=18, zorder=3)
    ax.text(16, -0.65, "Feature map", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=14, fontweight="bold", color="#444444")
    ax.text(7, -3, "×", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=24, color="#555555")
    ax.text(12.5, -3, "=", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=24, color="#555555")
    if pos is not None:
        r, k = pos
        frame(ax, k, -r, 3, 3)
        frame(ax, 14 + k, -1 - r, 1, 1)
        patch = img[r:r + 3, k:k + 3]
        terms = " + ".join(term(V_EDGE[i, j], patch[i, j]) for i in range(3) for j in range(3))
        prods = " + ".join(n(V_EDGE[i, j] * patch[i, j]) for i in range(3) for j in range(3))
        ax.text(-0.2, -6.75, f"Inner product of the filter and the highlighted patch  (output row {r + 1}, column {k + 1}):",
                ha="left", va="center", fontsize=14, color="#444444")
        ax.text(-0.2, -7.75, "z  =  " + terms, ha="left", va="center", fontsize=14, family="DejaVu Sans")
        ax.text(-0.2, -8.75, "    =  " + prods, ha="left", va="center", fontsize=14, family="DejaVu Sans")
        ax.text(-0.2, -9.75, f"    =  {n(OUT[r, k])}", ha="left", va="center", fontsize=15, fontweight="bold", color=RED)
    return fig


stack([slide_fig((p // 4, p % 4), p + 1) for p in range(16)])
```

Click to slide through all 16 positions. The left column of the filter subtracts and the right column adds, so the filter asks: **is it brighter on the right than on the left?** Once the filter reaches the end of a row, it drops down one pixel and starts again.

## The Same Calculation on a Real Photo

```{python}
# Block-average a 384 x 384 crop of the photo down to 64 x 64 and store whole-number pixels 0-255.
_g = load_sample_image("china.jpg").mean(axis=2)[0:384, 100:484]
PHOTO = np.rint(_g.reshape(64, 6, 64, 6).mean(axis=(1, 3))).astype(int)
assert PHOTO.shape == (64, 64) and PHOTO.min() >= 0 and PHOTO.max() <= 255

PHOTO_FILTERS = [("Vertical edges", V_EDGE, True), ("Horizontal edges", H_EDGE, True), ("Blur", BLUR, False),
                 ("Sharpen", SHARPEN, False), ("Outline", OUTLINE, True)]


def wfmt(w):
    return "1/9" if np.isclose(w, 1 / 9) else n(w)


def photo_fig(name, w, use_abs, Z, pos, done=()):
    """One frame: the photo, the zoomed patch, the filter, and the feature map showing only the pixels in done (pos None = finished)."""
    m = Z.shape[0]
    fig, ax = canvas((13.0, 6.9), (-0.3, 23.0), (-11.2, 1.0))
    # Input photo, drawn 7 units wide
    S = 7.0
    ax.imshow(PHOTO, cmap="gray", vmin=0, vmax=255, extent=(0, S, -S, 0), zorder=1, interpolation="nearest")
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((0, -S), S, S, fc="none", ec="#999999", lw=1, zorder=2))
    ax.text(S / 2, 0.35, f"Input photo: {PHOTO.shape[0]} × {PHOTO.shape[1]}", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=14, fontweight="bold", color="#444444")
    # Feature map, drawn the same size, showing only the pixels computed so far; the full map only at the end
    D = np.abs(Z) if use_abs else np.clip(Z, 0, 255)
    vmax = np.percentile(D, 99.5) if use_abs else 255
    shown = np.ma.masked_all(Z.shape)
    if pos is None:
        shown = np.ma.array(D)
    else:
        for rr, kk in done:
            shown[rr, kk] = D[rr, kk]
    cm = plt.get_cmap("gray").copy()
    cm.set_bad("#f3f3f3")
    X0 = 15.7
    ax.imshow(shown, cmap=cm, vmin=0, vmax=vmax, extent=(X0, X0 + S, -S, 0), zorder=1, interpolation="nearest")
    if pos is not None:
        q = S / m
        for rr, kk in done:          # outline each computed pixel so bright and dark ones both show
            ax.add_patch(Rectangle((X0 + kk * q, -(rr + 1) * q), q, q, fc="none", ec=BLUE, lw=0.9, zorder=3))
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((X0, -S), S, S, fc="none", ec="#999999", lw=1, zorder=2))
    ax.text(X0 + S / 2, 0.35, f"Feature map: {m} × {m}", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=14, fontweight="bold", color="#444444")
    count = m * m if pos is None else len(done)
    ax.text(X0 + S / 2, -S - 0.4, f"computed so far: {count:,} of {m * m:,} pixels", ha="center", va="top", fontsize=12.5, fontweight="bold", color=BLUE)
    ax.text(X0 + S / 2, -S - 1.05, ("brightness = |z|" if use_abs else "brightness = z, clipped to 0–255"), ha="center", va="top", fontsize=12, color="#555555")
    # Filter
    lim = np.abs(w).max() * 2
    cells(ax, w, x=11.55, y=-2.0, cmap="RdBu", vmin=-lim, vmax=lim, fs=15, fmt=wfmt, title=f"Filter: {name}", tfs=13)
    ax.text(10.95, -3.5, "×", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=22, color="#555555")
    ax.text(15.05, -3.5, "=", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=22, color="#555555")
    if pos is None:
        ax.text(-0.2, -8.6, f"Done: the filter visited all {m} × {m} = {m * m:,} positions, one inner product for each pixel of the feature map.",
                ha="left", va="center", fontsize=14, fontweight="bold", color=RED)
        ax.text(-0.2, -9.5, "Compare the feature map with the input photo to see what this filter picks out.", ha="left", va="center", fontsize=13.5, color="#444444")
        return fig
    r, k = pos
    px = S / PHOTO.shape[0]
    patch = PHOTO[r:r + 3, k:k + 3]
    # Box on the photo, its zoomed copy, and the matching output pixel
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((k * px, -(r + 3) * px), 3 * px, 3 * px, fc="none", ec=ORANGE, lw=2.6, zorder=5))
    cells(ax, patch, x=7.5, y=-2.0, cmap="gray", vmin=0, vmax=255, fs=13, title="Patch (zoomed)", tfs=13)
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((7.5, -5.0), 3, 3, fc="none", ec=ORANGE, lw=3, zorder=5))
    for yy in (0, 3):
        ax.plot([k * px + 3 * px, 7.5], [-(r + yy) * px, -2.0 - yy], color=ORANGE, lw=1.2, ls="--", zorder=4)
    qm = S / m   # the feature map has its own pixel size
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((X0 + k * qm - 0.12, -(r + 1) * qm - 0.12), qm + 0.24, qm + 0.24, fc="none", ec=ORANGE, lw=2.6, zorder=5))
    # The inner product, written out underneath
    ws, xs = w.ravel(), patch.ravel()
    groups = [" + ".join(f"({wfmt(ws[3 * i + j])})({xs[3 * i + j]})" for j in range(3)) for i in range(3)]
    if np.allclose(ws, ws[0]):   # blur: every weight is 1/9, so factor it out
        prods = f"(1/9)({' + '.join(str(v) for v in xs)})  =  (1/9)({xs.sum()})"
    else:
        vals = [a * b for a, b in zip(ws, xs)]
        prods = ("−" if vals[0] < 0 else "") + n(abs(vals[0]), 1)
        prods += "".join((" − " if v < 0 else " + ") + n(abs(v), 1) for v in vals[1:])
    ax.text(-0.2, -8.25, f"Inner product of the filter and the patch at output row {r + 1}, column {k + 1}:", ha="left", va="center", fontsize=13.5, color="#444444")
    ax.text(-0.2, -9.1, "z  =  " + groups[0] + "  +  " + groups[1] + "  +", ha="left", va="center", fontsize=13, family="DejaVu Sans")
    ax.text(-0.2, -9.8, "       " + groups[2], ha="left", va="center", fontsize=13, family="DejaVu Sans")
    ax.text(-0.2, -10.6, "    =  " + prods + "  =  ", ha="left", va="center", fontsize=13, family="DejaVu Sans")
    t = ax.texts[-1]
    fig.canvas.draw()
    bb = t.get_window_extent().transformed(ax.transData.inverted())
    ax.text(bb.x1, -10.6, n(Z[r, k], 1).replace("-", "−"), ha="left", va="center", fontsize=14, fontweight="bold", color=RED)
    return fig


# One filter (vertical edges, as on the last slide), sliding in reading order and stopping at 90 positions.
# Each stop works out one inner product, and only the pixels computed so far appear; the full feature map appears at the end.
name, w, use_abs = PHOTO_FILTERS[0]
Z = conv(PHOTO, w)
assert Z.shape == (62, 62)


def row_stops(r, strong=3, spread=2):
    """Columns to stop at on row r: the strongest edges (kept apart) plus a few evenly spaced ones, left to right."""
    cols = []
    for k in np.argsort(-np.abs(Z[r])):
        if len(cols) == strong:
            break
        if all(abs(k - c) >= 7 for c in cols):
            cols.append(int(k))
    for k in np.linspace(3, 58, spread + 2)[1:-1].astype(int):
        if all(abs(k - c) >= 5 for c in cols):
            cols.append(int(k))
    return sorted(cols)


stops = [(int(r), k) for r in np.linspace(2, 58, 24).astype(int) for k in row_stops(int(r), strong=4)]
stops = [stops[i] for i in np.unique(np.linspace(0, len(stops) - 1, 90).round().astype(int))]   # keep 90, spread over the photo
assert len(stops) == 90
frames, done = [], []
for r, k in stops:
    assert np.isclose(Z[r, k], (w * PHOTO[r:r + 3, k:k + 3]).sum())
    done.append((r, k))
    frames.append(photo_fig(name, w, use_abs, Z, (r, k), done))
frames.append(photo_fig(name, w, use_abs, Z, None))


stack(frames)
```

Click to slide the vertical-edge filter from slide 11 across a real photo: left to right, then down. Each click works out the inner product at one position, and only that pixel is added to the feature map. The last click shows the finished map, all 3,844 pixels: **bright exactly where the photo has vertical edges.**

## The Same Calculation on a Gray Image: Blur

```{python}
# A 29 x 21 pixel-art sprite, read cell by cell from the example in 3Blue1Brown's "But what is a convolution?"
SPRITE = """
.....................
.....................
.........KKKK.KKK....
.......KKRRRKKSSSK...
......KRRRRRRKSSSK...
.....KRRRKKKKKKSSK...
....KRRRKKKKKKKKSK...
....KRKKSSSSSSKKK....
...KKKKSSSKSKSKRRK...
...KSKKSSSKSKSKRRK...
..KSSKKKSSSSSSSKRK...
..KSSSKSSKSSSSSKRK...
...KSSSSKKKKSSKKK....
....KKSSSSKKKKKRK....
.....KKKSSSSSKRRK....
....KRRRKKKKKKRK.....
...KRRRRRKKRRKK......
..KRRRKKKBKRRRKK.....
..KRRKSSSKBKRRRK.....
..KRKSSSSSKBKKKKK....
...KKSSSSSKWWBBKK....
....KKSSSKBWWBKOOK...
...KOOKKKBBBBKOOOK...
..KKOKBBBBBBBKOOOK...
..KOOKBBBBKKKKOOOK...
..KOOKBKKK...KOOKK...
..KOOKK.......KKK....
...KK................
.....................
""".split()
PALETTE = {".": (128, 128, 128), "K": (0, 0, 0), "S": (255, 231, 160), "R": (215, 20, 4),
           "O": (186, 48, 11), "B": (46, 63, 169), "W": (255, 255, 255)}
MARIO = np.array([[PALETTE[ch] for ch in row] for row in SPRITE])
assert MARIO.shape == (29, 21, 3)


def grid_image(ax, A, x0, y0, u, done=None):
    """Draw an RGB grid with its top-left corner at (x0, y0) and cells of size u. If done is given, show only those cells."""
    h, wd = A.shape[:2]
    if done is None:
        ax.imshow(np.clip(A, 0, 255).astype(np.uint8), extent=(x0, x0 + wd * u, y0 - h * u, y0), interpolation="nearest", zorder=1)
    else:
        ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x0, y0 - h * u), wd * u, h * u, fc="#f3f3f3", ec="none", zorder=0.5))
        for rr, kk in done:
            ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x0 + kk * u, y0 - (rr + 1) * u), u, u, fc=np.clip(A[rr, kk], 0, 255) / 255, ec=BLUE, lw=0.9, zorder=3))
    for i in range(h + 1):
        ax.plot([x0, x0 + wd * u], [y0 - i * u] * 2, color="#d0d0d0", lw=0.5, zorder=2)
    for j in range(wd + 1):
        ax.plot([x0 + j * u] * 2, [y0, y0 - h * u], color="#d0d0d0", lw=0.5, zorder=2)


GRAY = np.rint(MARIO.mean(axis=2)).astype(int)    # one number per pixel: the average of R, G, B
GBLUR = conv(GRAY, BLUR)
assert GRAY.shape == (29, 21) and GBLUR.shape == (27, 19)


def as_rgb(G):
    """A gray grid as an RGB grid, so grid_image can draw it."""
    return np.stack([G] * 3, axis=2)


def gray_fig(pos, done):
    """One frame: the gray sprite, the zoomed patch, the blur filter, and the feature map showing only the cells in done (pos None = finished)."""
    fig, ax = canvas((13.0, 7.7), (-0.3, 23.0), (-12.9, 1.0))
    u = 8.2 / 29
    grid_image(ax, as_rgb(GRAY), 0, 0, u)
    ax.text(21 * u / 2, 0.35, "Input image: 29 × 21 (gray)", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=14, fontweight="bold", color="#444444")
    X0 = 17.2
    grid_image(ax, as_rgb(GBLUR), X0, -u, u, None if pos is None else done)
    ax.text(X0 + 19 * u / 2, 0.35, "Feature map: 27 × 19", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=14, fontweight="bold", color="#444444")
    cnt = 27 * 19 if pos is None else len(done)
    ax.text(X0 + 19 * u / 2, -28 * u - 0.15, f"computed so far: {cnt} of {27 * 19} pixels", ha="center", va="top", fontsize=12.5, fontweight="bold", color=BLUE)
    cells(ax, BLUR, x=11.35, y=-2.0, cmap="RdBu", vmin=-2 / 9, vmax=2 / 9, fs=15, fmt=lambda v: "1/9", title="Filter: Blur", tfs=13)
    ax.text(10.75, -3.5, "×", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=22, color="#555555")
    ax.text(15.6, -3.5, "=", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=22, color="#555555")
    if pos is None:
        ax.text(-0.2, -9.6, f"Done: the filter visited all 27 × 19 = {27 * 19} positions, one inner product at each one.",
                ha="left", va="center", fontsize=14, fontweight="bold", color=RED)
        ax.text(-0.2, -10.5, "Each output pixel is the average of the 3 × 3 block around it, so sharp edges turn into soft ones.",
                ha="left", va="center", fontsize=13.5, color="#444444")
        return fig
    r, k = pos
    patch = GRAY[r:r + 3, k:k + 3]
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((k * u, -(r + 3) * u), 3 * u, 3 * u, fc="none", ec=ORANGE, lw=2.8, zorder=5))
    cells(ax, patch, x=7.3, y=-2.0, cmap="gray", vmin=0, vmax=255, fs=13, title="Patch (zoomed)", tfs=13)
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((7.3, -5.0), 3, 3, fc="none", ec=ORANGE, lw=3, zorder=5))
    for yy in (0, 3):
        ax.plot([(k + 3) * u, 7.3], [-(r + yy) * u, -2.0 - yy], color=ORANGE, lw=1.2, ls="--", zorder=4)
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((X0 + k * u - 0.06, -u - (r + 1) * u - 0.06), u + 0.12, u + 0.12, fc="none", ec=ORANGE, lw=2.8, zorder=5))
    vals = patch.ravel()
    ax.text(-0.2, -9.1, f"Inner product of the filter and the patch (output row {r + 1}, column {k + 1}):",
            ha="left", va="center", fontsize=13.5, color="#444444")
    ax.text(-0.2, -9.9, f"z  =  (1/9)({' + '.join(str(v) for v in vals)})  =  (1/9)({vals.sum()})  =  {n(GBLUR[r, k], 1)}",
            ha="left", va="center", fontsize=13, family="DejaVu Sans")
    out = int(np.rint(GBLUR[r, k]))
    ax.text(-0.2, -10.9, f"Output pixel = {out}", ha="left", va="center", fontsize=14, fontweight="bold", color=RED)
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((3.6, -11.25), 0.7, 0.7, fc=str(np.clip(GBLUR[r, k], 0, 255) / 255), ec="#555555", lw=1, zorder=3))
    return fig


def gray_stops():
    """90 positions in reading order: rows 0, 2, ..., 26 (7 stops on the first six, 6 on the rest), favoring patches with the most change."""
    var = np.array([[GRAY[r:r + 3, k:k + 3].astype(float).std() for k in range(19)] for r in range(27)])
    out = []
    for r, per in zip(range(0, 27, 2), [7] * 6 + [6] * 8):
        cols = []
        for k in np.argsort(-var[r], kind="stable"):
            if len(cols) == per:
                break
            if all(abs(int(k) - c) >= 2 for c in cols):
                cols.append(int(k))
        for k in range(19):          # if spacing ran out of room, fill with the remaining columns
            if len(cols) == per:
                break
            if k not in cols:
                cols.append(k)
        out += [(r, k) for k in sorted(cols)]
    return out


gstops = gray_stops()
assert len(gstops) == 90
gframes, gdone = [], []
for r, k in gstops:
    assert np.isclose(GBLUR[r, k], GRAY[r:r + 3, k:k + 3].mean())
    gdone.append((r, k))
    gframes.append(gray_fig((r, k), list(gdone)))
gframes.append(gray_fig(None, gdone))
stack(gframes)
```

Start simple: make the sprite **gray**. Each pixel becomes **one number**, the average of its red, green and blue values. The 1/9 blur filter from 3Blue1Brown's video *But what is a convolution?* is a single 3 × 3 grid of weights (a filter of **depth 1**), and each position takes **one** inner product: the average of the 3 × 3 block under it. Click through 90 positions; the last click shows the whole feature map.

## The Same Calculation on a Color Image: Blur

```{python}
MBLUR = np.stack([conv(MARIO[:, :, ch], BLUR) for ch in range(3)], axis=2)    # blur each color channel separately
assert MBLUR.shape == (27, 19, 3)


def mario_fig(pos, done):
    """One frame: the sprite, the zoomed patch, the blur filter, and the blurred image showing only the cells in done (pos None = finished)."""
    fig, ax = canvas((13.0, 7.7), (-0.3, 23.0), (-12.9, 1.0))
    u = 8.2 / 29
    grid_image(ax, MARIO, 0, 0, u)
    ax.text(21 * u / 2, 0.35, "Input image: 29 × 21 (RGB)", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=14, fontweight="bold", color="#444444")
    X0 = 17.2
    grid_image(ax, MBLUR, X0, -u, u, None if pos is None else done)
    ax.text(X0 + 19 * u / 2, 0.35, "Blurred image: 27 × 19 (RGB)", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=14, fontweight="bold", color="#444444")
    cnt = 27 * 19 if pos is None else len(done)
    ax.text(X0 + 19 * u / 2, -28 * u - 0.15, f"computed so far: {cnt} of {27 * 19} pixels", ha="center", va="top", fontsize=12.5, fontweight="bold", color=BLUE)
    cells(ax, BLUR, x=11.35, y=-2.0, cmap="RdBu", vmin=-2 / 9, vmax=2 / 9, fs=15, fmt=lambda v: "1/9", title="Filter: Blur", tfs=13)
    ax.text(10.75, -3.5, "×", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=22, color="#555555")
    ax.text(15.6, -3.5, "=", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=22, color="#555555")
    if pos is None:
        ax.text(-0.2, -9.6, f"Done: the filter visited all 27 × 19 = {27 * 19} positions, three inner products (R, G, B) at each one.",
                ha="left", va="center", fontsize=14, fontweight="bold", color=RED)
        ax.text(-0.2, -10.5, "Each output pixel is the average of the 3 × 3 block around it, so sharp edges turn into soft ones.",
                ha="left", va="center", fontsize=13.5, color="#444444")
        return fig
    r, k = pos
    patch = MARIO[r:r + 3, k:k + 3]
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((k * u, -(r + 3) * u), 3 * u, 3 * u, fc="none", ec=ORANGE, lw=2.8, zorder=5))
    for i in range(3):
        for j in range(3):
            ax.add_patch(Rectangle((7.3 + j, -2.0 - i - 1), 1, 1, fc=patch[i, j] / 255, ec="#999999", lw=1, zorder=2))
    ax.text(8.8, -1.65, "Patch (zoomed)", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=13, fontweight="bold", color="#444444")
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((7.3, -5.0), 3, 3, fc="none", ec=ORANGE, lw=3, zorder=5))
    for yy in (0, 3):
        ax.plot([(k + 3) * u, 7.3], [-(r + yy) * u, -2.0 - yy], color=ORANGE, lw=1.2, ls="--", zorder=4)
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((X0 + k * u - 0.06, -u - (r + 1) * u - 0.06), u + 0.12, u + 0.12, fc="none", ec=ORANGE, lw=2.8, zorder=5))
    ax.text(-0.2, -9.1, f"Inner product of the filter with each color channel of the patch (output row {r + 1}, column {k + 1}):",
            ha="left", va="center", fontsize=13.5, color="#444444")
    for ch, (lab, col) in enumerate([("R", "#c0392b"), ("G", "#1a7f37"), ("B", "#1f4fd8")]):
        vals = patch[:, :, ch].ravel()
        ax.text(-0.2, -9.9 - 0.72 * ch, f"{lab}:", ha="left", va="center", fontsize=13, fontweight="bold", color=col)
        ax.text(0.5, -9.9 - 0.72 * ch, f"(1/9)({' + '.join(str(v) for v in vals)})  =  (1/9)({vals.sum()})  =  {n(MBLUR[r, k, ch], 1)}",
                ha="left", va="center", fontsize=13, family="DejaVu Sans")
    out = np.rint(MBLUR[r, k]).astype(int)

    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((5.6, -12.5), 0.7, 0.7, fc=np.clip(MBLUR[r, k], 0, 255) / 255, ec="#555555", lw=1, zorder=3))
    return fig


def mario_stops():
    """50 positions in reading order, favoring patches with the most color change, spread across each row."""
    var = np.array([[MARIO[r:r + 3, k:k + 3].astype(float).std() for k in range(19)] for r in range(27)])
    out = []
    for r, per in zip(range(1, 27, 3), [6, 6, 6, 6, 6, 5, 5, 5, 5]):
        cols = []
        for k in np.argsort(-var[r]):

                break
            if all(abs(int(k) - c) >= 2 for c in cols):
                cols.append(int(k))
        out += [(r, k) for k in sorted(cols)]
    return out


mstops = mario_stops()
assert len(mstops) == 50
mframes, mdone = [], []
for r, k in mstops:
    assert np.allclose(MBLUR[r, k], MARIO[r:r + 3, k:k + 3].reshape(9, 3).mean(axis=0))
    mdone.append((r, k))
    mframes.append(mario_fig((r, k), list(mdone)))
mframes.append(mario_fig(None, mdone))
stack(mframes)
```

Now the same 1/9 blur filter on the color image. A color image has three channels (red, green, blue). Here the filter slides over **each channel separately**, so every position takes three inner products and the output is still a color image. Click through 50 positions; the last click shows the whole blurred image.

## The Same Calculation on 1D Data: A Vertical Filter

```{python}
X1D = np.array([3, 4, 8, 6, 1, 5, 9, 7, 2, 0])      # 10 inputs, lined up like the input layer of a regular network
W1D = np.array([1, 1, 1]) / 3                        # a vertical 3 x 1 filter: the 1D version of the blur
Z1D = np.array([W1D @ X1D[i:i + 3] for i in range(len(X1D) - 2)])
assert len(Z1D) == 8 and np.allclose(Z1D, np.round(Z1D))


def oned_fig(pos, done):
    """One frame: the input column, the vertical filter, and the output column showing only the nodes in done (pos None = finished)."""
    fig, ax = canvas((13.0, 7.7), (-0.3, 23.0), (-12.9, 1.0))
    gap, rad = 1.15, 0.42
    xin, xout = 2.4, 9.2
    yin = [-0.8 - gap * i for i in range(10)]
    yout = [(yin[i] + yin[i + 2]) / 2 for i in range(8)]       # each output sits beside the middle of its 3 inputs
    ax.text(xin, 0.35, "Input layer: 10 numbers", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=14, fontweight="bold", color="#444444")
    ax.text(xout, 0.35, "Feature map: 8 numbers", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=14, fontweight="bold", color="#444444")
    # Connections: earlier positions in light grey, the current one in orange with its weights
    for i in done:
        cur = pos is not None and i == pos
        for j in range(3):
            ax.plot([xin + rad, xout - rad], [yin[i + j], yout[i]], color=ORANGE if cur else "#d6d6d6",
                    lw=2.4 if cur else 1.0, zorder=4 if cur else 1)
    # Input nodes
    for i, v in enumerate(X1D):
        hot = pos is not None and pos <= i < pos + 3
        ax.add_patch(plt.Circle((xin, yin[i]), rad, fc=FILL["in"], ec=ORANGE if hot else BLUE, lw=3 if hot else 1.5, zorder=5))
        ax.text(xin, yin[i], str(v), ha="center", va="center", fontsize=16, zorder=6)
        ax.text(xin - 0.62, yin[i], f"$x_{{{i + 1}}}$", ha="right", va="center", fontsize=14, color="#555555")
    # Output nodes: only those computed so far are filled in
    for i in range(8):
        shown = pos is None or i in done
        hot = pos is not None and i == pos
        ax.add_patch(plt.Circle((xout, yout[i]), rad, fc=FILL["out"] if shown else "#f3f3f3",
                                ec=ORANGE if hot else (GREEN if shown else "#bbbbbb"), lw=3 if hot else 1.5, zorder=5))
        if shown:
            ax.text(xout, yout[i], n(Z1D[i]), ha="center", va="center", fontsize=16, zorder=6)
        ax.text(xout + 0.62, yout[i], f"$z_{{{i + 1}}}$", ha="left", va="center", fontsize=14, color="#555555")
    cnt = 8 if pos is None else len(done)
    ax.text(xout, yin[-1] - 0.75, f"computed so far: {cnt} of 8", ha="center", va="top", fontsize=12.5, fontweight="bold", color=BLUE)
    # The filter, drawn as a vertical 3 x 1 grid
    cells(ax, W1D.reshape(3, 1), x=13.0, y=-1.2, cmap="RdBu", vmin=-2 / 3, vmax=2 / 3, fs=15, fmt=lambda v: "1/3",
          title="Filter: 3 × 1 (vertical)", tfs=13)
    if pos is None:
        ax.text(11.2, -6.0, "Done: the filter visited all 10 − 3 + 1 = 8 positions,", ha="left", va="center", fontsize=14, fontweight="bold", color=RED)
        ax.text(11.2, -6.75, "one inner product at each one.", ha="left", va="center", fontsize=14, fontweight="bold", color=RED)
        ax.text(11.2, -7.9, "Each output node is connected to only 3 neighboring inputs,", ha="left", va="center", fontsize=13.5, color="#444444")
        ax.text(11.2, -8.6, "and every output node uses the same 3 weights.", ha="left", va="center", fontsize=13.5, color="#444444")
        return fig
    i = pos
    xs = X1D[i:i + 3]
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((xin - rad - 0.12, yin[i + 2] - rad - 0.12), 2 * rad + 0.24, yin[i] - yin[i + 2] + 2 * rad + 0.24,
                           fc="none", ec=ORANGE, lw=2.6, zorder=6))
    ax.text(11.2, -6.0, f"Inner product of the filter and inputs $x_{{{i + 1}}}$, $x_{{{i + 2}}}$, $x_{{{i + 3}}}$  (output $z_{{{i + 1}}}$):",
            ha="left", va="center", fontsize=13.5, color="#444444")
    ax.text(11.2, -7.0, "z  =  " + " + ".join(f"(1/3)({v})" for v in xs), ha="left", va="center", fontsize=14, family="DejaVu Sans")
    ax.text(11.2, -7.9, f"    =  (1/3)({' + '.join(str(v) for v in xs)})  =  (1/3)({xs.sum()})", ha="left", va="center", fontsize=14, family="DejaVu Sans")
    ax.text(11.2, -8.9, f"    =  {n(Z1D[i])}", ha="left", va="center", fontsize=15, fontweight="bold", color=RED)
    return fig


oframes, odone = [], []
for p in range(8):
    assert np.isclose(Z1D[p], X1D[p:p + 3].mean())
    odone.append(p)
    oframes.append(oned_fig(p, list(odone)))
oframes.append(oned_fig(None, odone))
stack(oframes)
```

The same idea works for the 1D data of a regular network, where the input layer is a **vertical line** of numbers instead of a photo. The filter is now a **vertical 3 × 1** grid of weights, here the 1D blur (1/3, 1/3, 1/3). It slides **down** the column, one step at a time, and takes one inner product at each position. With 10 inputs and a filter of length 3, the feature map has 10 − 3 + 1 = 8 numbers. Click through all 8 positions.

## Do CNNs Work Well on Tabular Data?

**Usually not.** On ordinary tabular data (one row per customer, patient or house), tree-based models such as random forests, XGBoost and LightGBM usually beat CNNs.

| The CNN assumes... | Images | Tabular data |
|:------------------:|:------:|:------------:|
| **Locality:** neighbors belong together | Nearby pixels are related | Column order is arbitrary: age next to income next to zip code means nothing |
| **Repetition:** one filter is useful everywhere | An edge is an edge anywhere in the image | "$x_3 + x_4 + x_5$ is large" and "$x_7 + x_8 + x_9$ is large" mean different things |
| **Order matters** | Shuffle the pixels and the picture is gone | Shuffle the columns and nothing about the data changes, but the CNN's answer does |

-   Tabular data has other quirks that trees handle naturally: categorical and numeric features mixed together, skewed values, useless columns, and sharp cutoffs such as "income > 50K".
-   **Exception:** some tables are really signals in disguise, such as readings over time, spectra, or positions along a gene. The column order then carries meaning, and a 1D CNN can work well.

::: {.check}
**Your turn.** Shuffle the 10 inputs on the last slide. Does the feature map still mean anything? Would a random forest change if we shuffled the columns of its data?
:::

::: {.key}
A convolution helps only when **the order of the inputs carries information.** Images have it; most tables do not.
:::

::: {.note}
Grinsztajn, Oyallon and Varoquaux (2022), *Why do tree-based models still outperform deep learning on tabular data?* Shwartz-Ziv and Armon (2022), *Tabular data: Deep learning is not all you need.*
:::

## Why Is It Called "Convolutional"?

-   The name comes from a math operation called **convolution** (from the Latin *convolvere*, "to roll together"). It shows up in calculus, signal processing and probability.
-   Discrete convolution of a list $x$ with a short filter $w$: **slide, multiply, add.**

$$(x * w)_i = \sum_{k} x_{i-k}\, w_k \qquad\qquad (f * g)(t) = \int f(\tau)\, g(t - \tau)\, d\tau \;\;\text{(continuous version)}$$

-   You already know one use from probability: the distribution of the sum of two dice. With $X$ and $Y$ independent,

$$P(X + Y = s) = \sum_{k} P(X = k)\, P(Y = s - k)$$

-   A CNN layer does the same slide, multiply and add. With the 3 × 1 filter $(w_1, w_2, w_3)$ from the 1D slide:

| | Output at position $i$ |
|:--:|:--:|
| **What a CNN computes** | $z_i = w_1 x_i + w_2 x_{i+1} + w_3 x_{i+2}$ |
| **Textbook convolution** | $z_i = w_3 x_i + w_2 x_{i+1} + w_1 x_{i+2}$ (the filter is **flipped**) |

-   Strictly, the CNN version is called **cross-correlation**. The flip makes no difference in practice: the weights are learned, so the network would simply learn the flipped filter. The name "convolution" stuck.

::: {.key}
A **convolutional** neural network is a network whose layers are built from convolutions: **one small set of weights slides across the input**, and at every position it takes the same multiply-and-add we have used since the linear model.
:::

## What the Filter Is Really Doing: Matching a Pattern

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="56%"}
```{python}
patches = [("Dark to light", np.array([[0, 0, 1]] * 3)), ("Flat", np.array([[1, 1, 1]] * 3)), ("Light to dark", np.array([[1, 0, 0]] * 3)), ("Horizontal edge", np.array([[0, 0, 0], [1, 1, 1], [1, 1, 1]]))]
scores = [float((p * V_EDGE).sum()) for _, p in patches]
assert scores == [3.0, 0.0, -3.0, 0.0]
fig, ax = canvas((8.3, 3.15), (-0.2, 20.2), (-5.7, 1.5))
for i, ((nm, p), s) in enumerate(zip(patches, scores)):
    x = i * 5.2
    cells(ax, p, x=x, cmap="gray", vmin=0, vmax=1, fs=14, title=nm, tfs=11.5)
    ax.text(x + 1.5, -4.2, f"z = {n(s)}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=17, fontweight="bold", color=RED if s > 0 else INK)
show_fig(fig)
```

The output is large when the patch looks like the filter. Mathematically it is a dot product: it measures how well two grids of numbers line up.
:::

::: {.column width="44%"}
| Patch vs. filter | $z$ |
|:---------:|:---:|
| Same pattern | large and positive |
| No pattern | near 0 |
| Opposite pattern | large and negative |

-   So **a filter is a pattern detector**, and the feature map is a map of where the pattern occurs.
-   ReLU then keeps only the positive matches: $\max(0, z)$.
:::
::::

::: {.key}
Look back at the feature map: columns of 0, 3, 3, 0. It lights up only along the edge in the image. One filter with **9 weights** found the edge, wherever it was.
:::

## It Is Still Our Same Node

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
```{python}
vals = img[0:3, 2:5].ravel()
wts = V_EDGE.ravel()
fig, ax = canvas((8.8, 5.6), (-4.8, 4.25), (-3.0, 2.75))
ys = np.linspace(2.2, -2.6, 10)
labels = ["1"] + [n(v) for v in vals]
weights = ["$b$"] + [f"${n(w)}$" for w in wts]
Rn, split = 1.05, 0.12
for y, lab, wtxt, i in zip(ys, labels, weights, range(10)):
    ax.add_patch(plt.Circle((-3.8, y), 0.22, fc=FILL["grey"] if i == 0 else FILL["in"], ec=GREY if i == 0 else BLUE, lw=1.6, zorder=5))
    ax.text(-3.8, y, lab, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=13.5, zorder=6)
    d = np.hypot(3.8, y)
    arrow(ax, -3.8 + 0.22 * 3.8 / d, y - 0.22 * y / d, -Rn * 3.8 / d, Rn * y / d, lw=1.2)
    ax.text(-2.75, y * 0.72, wtxt, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=13, zorder=6, bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.08", fc="white", ec="none"))
ax.add_patch(plt.Circle((0, 0), Rn, fc=FILL["hid"], ec=ORANGE, lw=2.4, zorder=3))
half = np.sqrt(Rn ** 2 - split ** 2)
ax.plot([split, split], [-half, half], color=ORANGE, lw=2.4, zorder=4)
ax.text(-0.42, 0, r"$\Sigma$", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=25, zorder=5)
activation_icon(ax, 0.6, 0, 0.62, 0.85, ORANGE, lw=2.6)
arrow(ax, Rn, 0, 2.1, 0)
ax.text(2.2, 0, "$h_{ij}$", ha="left", va="center", fontsize=19)
ax.text(-3.8, 2.6, "patch", ha="center", fontsize=13, fontweight="bold", color="#444444")
ax.text(-2.75, 2.6, "weights", ha="center", fontsize=13, fontweight="bold", color="#444444")
ax.text(0, 1.3, "add, then ReLU", ha="center", fontsize=13, fontweight="bold", color="#444444")
show_fig(fig)
```
:::

::: {.column width="42%"}
Each output is one node, with 9 pixels as its inputs, a bias $b$, and a ReLU activation.

$$z_{ij} = b + \sum_{k=1}^{3} \sum_{l=1}^{3} w_{kl}\, x_{i+k-1,\ j+l-1}$$

$$h_{ij} = \max(0,\ z_{ij})$$

Here $x_{ij}$ is the pixel in row $i$ and column $j$, and $h_{ij}$ is the output for the patch starting there.

The **only** subscripts on $w$ are the positions inside the filter. There is no $i$ or $j$ on $w$: every position uses the same weights.
:::
::::

::: {.note}
Strictly, this operation is called cross-correlation, because mathematical convolution also flips the filter. Deep learning uses the name "convolution" anyway. The worked examples in this deck set $b = 0$ unless stated.
:::

## From Fully Connected to Convolution, in Two Steps

```{python}
def wiring(ax, mode, title, count):
    n_in, n_out = 7, 5
    xin = np.arange(n_in) * 1.0
    xout = 1 + np.arange(n_out) * 1.0
    colors = [BLUE, ORANGE, GREEN]
    for j, xo in enumerate(xout):
        for i, xi in enumerate(xin):
            near = j <= i <= j + 2
            if mode == "full":
                ax.plot([xi, xo], [0, 2.3], color="#999999", lw=1.0, zorder=1)
            elif near:
                col = colors[i - j] if mode == "shared" else "#777777"
                ax.plot([xi, xo], [0, 2.3], color=col, lw=2.2, zorder=1)
    ax.scatter(xin, [0] * n_in, s=190, fc=FILL["in"], ec=BLUE, lw=1.6, zorder=3)
    ax.scatter(xout, [2.3] * n_out, s=190, fc=FILL["hid"], ec=ORANGE, lw=1.6, zorder=3)
    ax.set_xlim(-0.6, 6.6)
    ax.set_ylim(-0.75, 3.1)
    ax.axis("off")
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=15.5, fontweight="bold", color="#444444")
    ax.text(3, -0.55, count, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=14.5, color=INK)


assert fc_params(7, 5) == 40 and fc_params(3, 5) == 20 and fc_params(3, 1) == 4
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13.2, 3.75))
wiring(ax[0], "full", "Fully connected", "(7 + 1) × 5 = 40 parameters")
wiring(ax[1], "local", "Step 1: local connections", "(3 + 1) × 5 = 20 parameters")
wiring(ax[2], "shared", "Step 2: and shared weights", "3 + 1 = 4 parameters")
fig.tight_layout()
show_fig(fig)
```

```{python}
assert fc_params(784, 676) == 530660 and (9 + 1) * 676 == 6760 and conv_params(3, 1, 1) == 10
table(["28 × 28 image → 26 × 26 output", "Fully connected", "Local connections", "Local and shared (one 3 × 3 filter)"],
      [["Parameters", "(784 + 1) × 676 = " + c(fc_params(784, 676)), "(9 + 1) × 676 = " + c(6760), "9 + 1 = **10**"]])
```

The picture shows one row of pixels, with bias nodes not drawn. In the right panel, arrows of the same color share one weight.

::: {.key}
**A convolutional layer is a fully connected layer with rules:** most weights are forced to 0, and the rest are forced to be equal. Like LASSO, it limits the weights to fight overfitting. LASSO learns which weights to zero out. Here **we** decide, using what we know about images.
:::

## Filters on a Real Photo

```{python}
panels = [("Original photo", None, china), ("Vertical edges", V_EDGE, np.abs(conv(china, V_EDGE, mode="same"))),
          ("Horizontal edges", H_EDGE, np.abs(conv(china, H_EDGE, mode="same"))), ("Blur", BLUR, conv(china, BLUR, mode="same")),
          ("Sharpen", SHARPEN, conv(china, SHARPEN, mode="same")), ("Outline", OUTLINE, np.abs(conv(china, OUTLINE, mode="same")))]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(13.0, 6.1))
for a, (title, w, im) in zip(axes.ravel(), panels):
    crop = im[3:-3, 3:-3]
    if w is None or title in ("Blur", "Sharpen"):
        a.imshow(crop, cmap="gray", vmin=0, vmax=1)
    else:
        a.imshow(crop, cmap="gray", vmin=0, vmax=np.percentile(crop, 99.5))
    a.set_title(title, fontsize=15, fontweight="bold", color="#444444")
    a.axis("off")
    if w is not None:
        ins = a.inset_axes([0.0, 0.0, 0.2, 0.3])
        ins.set_xlim(0, 3)
        ins.set_ylim(-3, 0)
        ins.axis("off")
        lim = np.abs(w).max() * 2
        cells(ins, w, cmap="RdBu", vmin=-lim, vmax=lim, fs=10, fmt=lambda v: "1/9" if np.isclose(v, 1 / 9) else n(v), lw=0.6)
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=1.4)
show_fig(fig)
```

Each result comes from a single $3 \times 3$ filter, shown in the corner of the panel. For the edge and outline panels, brighter means a stronger response (we plot $|z|$).

## Key Point: Nobody Chooses the Filters

```{python}
rand, trained = R["cnn_filters_random"][:, 0], R["cnn_filters_trained"][:, 0]
assert rand.shape == (16, 3, 3) and np.abs(trained).mean() > np.abs(rand).mean()
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 9, figsize=(12.6, 3.25), gridspec_kw=dict(width_ratios=[1] * 8 + [1.6]))
for a in axes.ravel():
    a.axis("off")
lim = max(np.abs(rand).max(), np.abs(trained).max())
for i in range(8):
    axes[0, i].imshow(rand[i], cmap="RdBu", vmin=-lim, vmax=lim)
    axes[1, i].imshow(trained[i], cmap="RdBu", vmin=-lim, vmax=lim)
axes[0, 8].text(0, 0.5, "Before training\n(random start)", ha="left", va="center", fontsize=14, fontweight="bold", color="#444444", transform=axes[0, 8].transAxes)
axes[1, 8].text(0, 0.5, "After training\non real digits", ha="left", va="center", fontsize=14, fontweight="bold", color="#444444", transform=axes[1, 8].transAxes)
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.01, right=0.995, top=0.98, bottom=0.02, wspace=0.08, hspace=0.08)
show_fig(fig)
```

-   Before about 2012, experts designed filters like the ones on the last slide by hand, then fed the results to a classifier.
-   In a CNN, the numbers in a filter are simply **weights**. They start out random, and gradient descent changes them to lower the loss, exactly as in Step 3 of our framework.
-   These are 8 of the 16 filters from a real CNN we trained on MNIST. Red is negative and blue is positive. Training has made their weights larger and given many of them a clearer pattern.

::: {.key}
The network **learns what to look for**. Its features are not designed by a person; they are found because they reduce the loss.
:::

## Two Settings: Padding and Stride

```{python}
assert out_size(5, 3) == 3 and out_size(5, 3, p=1) == 5 and out_size(5, 3, p=1, s=2) == 3
assert out_size(28, 3) == 26 and out_size(28, 3, p=1) == 28 and out_size(32, 5) == 28 and out_size(224, 7, p=3, s=2) == 112


def pad_panel(ax, title, sub, pad, frames, stride_note=None):
    size = 5 + 2 * pad
    ax.set_xlim(-0.4, 7.4)
    ax.set_ylim(-8.1, 0.3)
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.axis("off")
    off = 1 - pad
    for r in range(size):
        for k in range(size):
            inner = pad <= r < 5 + pad and pad <= k < 5 + pad
            ax.add_patch(Rectangle((off + k, -off - r - 1), 1, 1, fc="#dfe8ff" if inner else "#f3f3f3", ec="#aaaaaa" if inner else "#cccccc", lw=1, ls="-" if inner else "--", zorder=1))
            if not inner:
                ax.text(off + k + 0.5, -off - r - 0.5, "0", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=11, color=GREY)
    for (r, k), col, lw in frames:
        ax.add_patch(Rectangle((off + k, -off - r - 3), 3, 3, fc="none", ec=col, lw=lw, zorder=4))
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=15.5, fontweight="bold", color="#444444")
    ax.text(3.5, -7.65, sub, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=14)


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(11.6, 4.1))
pad_panel(axes[0], "No padding, stride 1", "5 × 5 becomes 3 × 3", 0, [((0, 0), ORANGE, 3.5), ((0, 1), BLUE, 2.5)])
pad_panel(axes[1], "Padding 1, stride 1", "5 × 5 stays 5 × 5", 1, [((0, 0), ORANGE, 3.5), ((0, 1), BLUE, 2.5)])
pad_panel(axes[2], "Padding 1, stride 2", "5 × 5 becomes 3 × 3", 1, [((0, 0), ORANGE, 3.5), ((0, 2), BLUE, 2.5)])
fig.tight_layout()
show_fig(fig)
```

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
-   **Padding $p$:** add a border of zeros, so the output does not shrink and the edges are not ignored.
-   **Stride $s$:** how many pixels the filter jumps each time. A larger stride makes the output smaller.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
For an $n \times n$ input and an $f \times f$ filter, the output size is

$$\left\lfloor \frac{n - f + 2p}{s} \right\rfloor + 1$$
:::
::::
