## Max Pooling: Keep the Strongest Signal, Shrink the Map

```{python}
Mx = np.array([[1, 0, 2, 3], [4, 6, 1, 8], [3, 1, 0, 0], [1, 2, 2, 4]])
assert (pool(Mx) == np.array([[6, 8], [3, 4]])).all()
peak_a, peak_b = np.zeros((4, 4)), np.zeros((4, 4))
peak_a[0, 0], peak_b[1, 1] = 9, 9
peak_c = np.zeros((4, 4))
peak_c[1, 2] = 9
assert (pool(peak_a) == pool(peak_b)).all() and not (pool(peak_a) == pool(peak_c)).all()
fig, ax = canvas((12.6, 3.45), (-0.3, 26.6), (-5.2, 1.6))
tints = np.array([[0, 0, 1, 1], [0, 0, 1, 1], [2, 2, 3, 3], [2, 2, 3, 3]])
TINT = ["#dfe8ff", "#FDE3C8", "#dcf3e2", "#f3e5f7"]
for r in range(4):
    for k in range(4):
        ax.add_patch(Rectangle((k, -r - 1), 1, 1, fc=TINT[tints[r, k]], ec="#999999", zorder=2))
        ax.text(k + 0.5, -r - 0.5, n(Mx[r, k]), ha="center", va="center", fontsize=16, zorder=3)
ax.text(2, 0.35, "Feature map: 4 × 4", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=14, fontweight="bold", color="#444444")
arrow(ax, 4.3, -2, 6.0, -2)
ax.text(5.15, -1.35, "max", ha="center", fontsize=13.5, color="#444444")
for r in range(2):
    for k in range(2):
        ax.add_patch(Rectangle((6.3 + k, -1 - r - 1), 1, 1, fc=TINT[r * 2 + k], ec="#999999", zorder=2))
        ax.text(6.8 + k, -1 - r - 0.5, n(pool(Mx)[r, k]), ha="center", va="center", fontsize=17, zorder=3)
ax.text(7.3, -0.65, "2 × 2", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=14, fontweight="bold", color="#444444")
ax.plot([10.6, 10.6], [-5.0, 1.3], color="#dddddd", lw=1.4)
for x, m, t in [(11.6, peak_a, "A pattern here"), (18.8, peak_b, "Moved by one pixel")]:
    cells(ax, m, x=x, cmap="Oranges", vmin=0, vmax=14, fs=14, text=False, title=t)
    r_, k_ = np.argwhere(m == 9)[0]
    ax.text(x + k_ + 0.5, -r_ - 0.5, "9", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=16, zorder=4)
    arrow(ax, x + 4.1, -2, x + 4.8, -2)
    cells(ax, pool(m), x=x + 4.9, y=-1, cmap="Oranges", vmin=0, vmax=14, fs=16)
show_fig(fig)
```

-   **What it does:** in each $2 \times 2$ block, keep only the largest value. Width and height are cut in half.
-   **No parameters:** pooling has no weights, so there is nothing to learn. It also makes later layers cheaper.
-   **Tolerance:** a pattern can move a little and pooling gives the same answer, as on the right. This holds only while the pattern stays in the same block, so it helps with small shifts but does not remove the problem.

::: {.key}
A feature map says "there is an edge at this exact pixel." After pooling it says "there is an edge **around here**", and that is usually all we need.
:::

# Part 3. From 2D to 3D

## How 3D Enters: Two Ways

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.view}
Way 1: from the filters
:::

One filter finds one pattern, but we need many: edges at every angle, spots, stripes. Each filter makes its own 2D feature map. Stack the maps, and the output has **height, width and depth**.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.view}
Way 2: from the data
:::

A color image has three numbers per pixel: red, green, blue. So it already comes as a stack of three 2D grids: **height, width and depth**.
:::
::::

```{python}
filters4 = [("vertical\nedge", V_EDGE), ("horizontal\nedge", H_EDGE), ("diagonal\nedge", np.array([[0, 1, 1], [-1, 0, 1], [-1, -1, 0]])), ("spot", np.array([[-1, -1, -1], [-1, 8, -1], [-1, -1, -1]]))]
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(13.0, 3.55))
ax = fig.add_axes([0, 0, 1, 1])
ax.set_xlim(-0.5, 36.5)
ax.set_ylim(-0.8, 9.1)
ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.axis("off")
ax.set_autoscale_on(False)
ax.imshow(digit, cmap="gray", extent=(0, 6, 0.8, 6.8), vmin=0, vmax=1, zorder=2)
ax.text(3, 7.2, "28 × 28 × 1", ha="center", fontsize=14, fontweight="bold", color="#444444")
ax.text(3, -0.15, "gray image: depth 1", ha="center", fontsize=13, color="#444444")
for i, (nm, w) in enumerate(filters4):
    x = 8.5 + i * 3.45
    m = relu(conv(digit, w, mode="same"))
    ax.imshow(m, cmap="magma", extent=(x, x + 2.9, 2.2, 5.1), zorder=2)
    ax.text(x + 1.45, 1.75, nm, ha="center", va="top", fontsize=12, color="#444444", linespacing=1.15)
ax.text(8.5 + 1.5 * 3.45 + 1.45, 6.4, "4 filters give 4 feature maps", ha="center", fontsize=14, fontweight="bold", color="#444444")
arrow(ax, 6.4, 3.7, 8.2, 3.7)
arrow(ax, 22.4, 3.7, 24.0, 3.7)
for i in range(3, -1, -1):
    x, y = 24.4 + i * 1.05, 0.9 + i * 0.72
    ax.imshow(relu(conv(digit, filters4[i][1], mode="same")), cmap="magma", extent=(x, x + 4.6, y, y + 4.6), zorder=3 + (3 - i))
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x, y), 4.6, 4.6, fc="none", ec="#555555", lw=1.2, zorder=3 + (3 - i)))
ax.text(29.3, 8.2, "stacked: 28 × 28 × 4", ha="center", fontsize=14, fontweight="bold", color="#444444")
ax.text(29.3, -0.15, "height × width × depth", ha="center", fontsize=13, color="#444444")
show_fig(fig)
```

::: {.key}
From now on, data inside a CNN is a **3D array** (a tensor): $H \times W \times C$. The depth $C$ is the number of **channels**. Every layer takes in a 3D array and puts out a 3D array.
:::

## A Color Image Is a Stack of Three Grids

```{python}
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(13.2, 3.75))
gs = fig.add_gridspec(1, 5, width_ratios=[1.25, 1, 1, 1, 1.15], wspace=0.08, left=0.01, right=0.99, top=0.9, bottom=0.02)
a = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 0])
a.imshow(flower)
a.set_title("The photo", fontsize=15, fontweight="bold", color="#444444")
a.axis("off")
for j, (nm, cm) in enumerate([("Red channel", None), ("Green channel", None), ("Blue channel", None)]):
    a = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, j + 1])
    a.imshow(flower[:, :, j], cmap="gray", vmin=0, vmax=1)
    a.set_title(nm, fontsize=15, fontweight="bold", color="#444444")
    a.axis("off")
a = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 4])
a.set_xlim(0, 10)
a.set_ylim(0, 8.6)
a.set_aspect("equal")
a.axis("off")
for i, col in [(2, "#c9d8ff"), (1, "#c5ecd0"), (0, "#ffc9c4")]:
    a.add_patch(Rectangle((1 + i * 1.2, 1 + i * 0.9), 5.6, 4.2, fc=col, ec="#555555", lw=1.3, zorder=3 - i))
a.text(3.8, 3.1, "R", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=16, zorder=5)
a.text(5.0, 5.55, "G", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=14, zorder=5)
a.text(6.2, 6.45, "B", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=14, zorder=5)
a.text(5, 0.25, "H × W × 3", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=15, fontweight="bold", color="#444444")
show_fig(fig)
```

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
Each channel is a grayscale grid: bright where that color is strong. The flower is bright in red, medium in green and dark in blue. In numbers, that is what "orange" means.
:::

::: {.column width="52%"}
| Data | Shape $H \times W \times C$ |
|:-----:|:------:|
| A grayscale digit | $28 \times 28 \times 1$ |
| A color photo | $224 \times 224 \times 3$ |
| Feature maps inside a network | $56 \times 56 \times 64$ |
:::
::::

## A Filter on 3D Data Has 3D Weights

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{python}
fig, ax = canvas((8.4, 5.3), (-0.8, 15.8), (-1.6, 9.0))
for i, (fc, ec) in reversed(list(enumerate([("#ffd9d6", RED), ("#d6f2dd", GREEN), ("#d9e4ff", BLUE)]))):
    ox, oy = i * 0.65, i * 0.48
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((ox, oy), 6, 6, fc=fc, ec=ec, lw=1.5, zorder=3 - i))
    for t in range(1, 6):
        ax.plot([ox + t, ox + t], [oy, oy + 6], color=ec, lw=0.45, zorder=3 - i)
        ax.plot([ox, ox + 6], [oy + t, oy + t], color=ec, lw=0.45, zorder=3 - i)
block(ax, 1, 3, 3, 3, 2, fc=ORANGE, ec="#a8551c", lw=1.5, z=6, ox=0.65, oy=0.48)
ax.text(2.5, 4.5, "3 × 3 × 3\nfilter", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=13, color="white", fontweight="bold", zorder=8)
arrow(ax, 5.2, 4.5, 7.4, 4.5, color=INK, lw=2.5, z=9)
arrow(ax, 2.5, 2.7, 2.5, 0.5, color=INK, lw=2.5, z=9)
ax.text(3.5, 8.2, "Input: 6 × 6 × 3", ha="center", fontsize=14.5, fontweight="bold", color="#444444")
ax.text(2.9, -0.55, "slides in 2 directions only", ha="center", fontsize=14, color=INK)
arrow(ax, 8.7, 3.1, 10.3, 3.1)
for t in range(5):
    ax.plot([11 + t, 11 + t], [0.6, 4.6], color="#b26a35", lw=0.6, zorder=2)
    ax.plot([11, 15], [0.6 + t, 0.6 + t], color="#b26a35", lw=0.6, zorder=2)
ax.add_patch(Rectangle((11, 0.6), 4, 4, fc=FILL["hid"], ec=ORANGE, lw=1.6, zorder=1))
ax.add_patch(Rectangle((12, 3.6), 1, 1, fc=ORANGE, ec="#a8551c", lw=1.5, zorder=3))
ax.text(13, 5.4, "Output: 4 × 4\none filter, one map", ha="center", fontsize=14, fontweight="bold", color="#444444", linespacing=1.3)
show_fig(fig)
```
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
-   The filter's depth **always matches** the depth of its input. On a color image, it has one $3 \times 3$ grid of weights **per channel**: 27 weights.
-   All 27 products are added to give **one number**, so one filter still gives one 2D map.
-   It still slides in **2 directions** only: across and down. There is nowhere to slide in depth, because it already covers all of it.

$$z_{ij} = b + \sum_{k} \sum_{l} \sum_{c=1}^{C} w_{klc}\, x_{i+k-1,\ j+l-1,\ c}$$

The only change from 2D is one more sum, over the channels.
:::
::::

## Worked Example: One Position on a Color Image

```{python}
PR, PG, PB = np.array([[3, 1], [2, 0]]), np.array([[1, 2], [0, 3]]), np.array([[1, 1], [2, 2]])
WR, WG, WB = np.array([[1, -1], [1, -1]]), np.array([[-1, 1], [-1, 1]]), np.array([[1, 0], [0, -1]])
b3 = -2
sr, sg, sb = (PR * WR).sum(), (PG * WG).sum(), (PB * WB).sum()
z3 = b3 + sr + sg + sb
assert (sr, sg, sb, z3) == (4, 4, -1, 5) and conv_params(2, 3, 1) == 13


def color_fig(done):
    fig, ax = canvas((8.1, 5.6), (-2.2, 12.8), (-9.0, 1.2))
    for i, (nm, p, w, s, tint) in enumerate([("Red", PR, WR, sr, "#ffd9d6"), ("Green", PG, WG, sg, "#d6f2dd"), ("Blue", PB, WB, sb, "#d9e4ff")]):
        y = -i * 3.2
        ax.text(-0.3, y - 1, nm, ha="right", va="center", fontsize=14.5, fontweight="bold", color="#444444")
        cells(ax, p, x=0, y=y, face=tint, fs=16, title="patch" if i == 0 else None)
        ax.text(3, y - 1, "×", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=20, color="#555555")
        cells(ax, w, x=4, y=y, cmap="RdBu", vmin=-2.4, vmax=2.4, fs=16, title="weights" if i == 0 else None)
        ax.text(7, y - 1, "=", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=20, color="#555555")
        if i < done:
            ax.text(7.7, y - 1, n(s), ha="left", va="center", fontsize=20, color=RED, fontweight="bold")
    return fig

```

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}
```{python}
stack([color_fig(i) for i in range(4)])
```
:::

::: {.column width="53%"}
```{python}
steps([
    r"A $2 \times 2 \times 3$ filter sits on one patch of a color image. It has 12 weights and a bias $b = -2$.",
    rf"**Red:** $({WR[0,0]})({PR[0,0]}) + ({WR[0,1]})({PR[0,1]}) + ({WR[1,0]})({PR[1,0]}) + ({WR[1,1]})({PR[1,1]}) = {sr}$",
    rf"**Green:** $({WG[0,0]})({PG[0,0]}) + ({WG[0,1]})({PG[0,1]}) + ({WG[1,0]})({PG[1,0]}) + ({WG[1,1]})({PG[1,1]}) = {sg}$",
    rf"**Blue:** $({WB[0,0]})({PB[0,0]}) + ({WB[0,1]})({PB[0,1]}) + ({WB[1,0]})({PB[1,0]}) + ({WB[1,1]})({PB[1,1]}) = {sb}$",
    rf"**Add, with the bias:** $z = {b3} + {sr} + {sg} + ({sb}) = {z3}$. **ReLU:** $h = \max(0, {z3}) = {z3}$.",
    r"Three channels go in and **one number** comes out. This filter has $2 \times 2 \times 3 + 1 = 13$ parameters.",
])
```
:::
::::

## What Color Filters Can See

```{python}
gray = flower.mean(axis=2)
WC = np.stack([np.ones((3, 3)) / 9, -np.ones((3, 3)) / 9, np.zeros((3, 3))], axis=2)
resp = sum(conv(flower[:, :, ch], WC[:, :, ch], mode="same") for ch in range(3))[2:-2, 2:-2]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13.0, 3.95))
ax[0].imshow(flower)
ax[1].imshow(gray, cmap="gray", vmin=0, vmax=1)
ax[2].imshow(relu(resp), cmap="magma")
for a, t in zip(ax, ["Color photo", "Grayscale: color is gone", "One 3 × 3 × 3 filter: red minus green"]):
    a.set_title(t, fontsize=15, fontweight="bold", color="#444444")
    a.axis("off")
fig.tight_layout()
show_fig(fig)
```

-   This filter has weights $+\tfrac{1}{9}$ on red, $-\tfrac{1}{9}$ on green and $0$ on blue, so its output is high where a patch is **more red than green**.
-   A filter on a grayscale image could not do this: that image no longer records color at all.

::: {.key}
Weights across channels let a single filter combine **shape and color**, such as "a red-to-green edge."
:::

## Counting Parameters: The Same Rule as Before

```{python}
assert conv_params(3, 1, 16) == 160 and conv_params(3, 3, 64) == 1792 and conv_params(3, 16, 32) == 4640 and conv_params(11, 3, 96) == 34944
```

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="37%"}
A fully connected node sees $m$ inputs. A filter sees $f \times f \times C$ inputs:

$$\underbrace{(m + 1) \times k}_{\text{fully connected}} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \underbrace{(f \times f \times C + 1) \times k}_{\text{convolutional}}$$

-   $f$: filter size
-   $C$: depth of the **input**
-   $k$: number of filters, which is the depth of the **output**
-   The $+1$ is each filter's bias
:::

::: {.column width="63%"}
```{python}
table(["Input", "Layer", "Calculation", "Parameters"], [
    [r"$28 \times 28 \times 1$", "16 filters, 3 × 3", r"$(3 \times 3 \times 1 + 1) \times 16$", "160"],
    [r"$224 \times 224 \times 3$", "64 filters, 3 × 3", r"$(3 \times 3 \times 3 + 1) \times 64$", "1,792"],
    [r"$14 \times 14 \times 16$", "32 filters, 3 × 3", r"$(3 \times 3 \times 16 + 1) \times 32$", "4,640"],
    [r"$224 \times 224 \times 3$", "96 filters, 11 × 11", r"$(11 \times 11 \times 3 + 1) \times 96$", "34,944"],
])
```

Compare the second row with the 150 million from Part 1 for the same image.
:::
::::

::: {.key}
**Height and width do not appear in the rule.** The same filter slides over any image size, so a bigger photo does not need more convolutional parameters.
:::

## Why Depth Matters: Layer 2 Reads Layer 1

::: {.h400}
```{python}
sq = np.zeros((10, 10))
sq[2:8, 2:8] = 1
mv = relu(conv(sq, V_EDGE, mode="same"))
mh = relu(conv(sq, H_EDGE, mode="same"))
z_corner = mv + mh - 3
corner = relu(z_corner)
assert (corner > 0).sum() == 1 and corner[2, 2] == 1 and mv[2, 2] == 2 and mh[2, 2] == 2


def corner_fig(stage):
    fig, ax = canvas((13.4, 4.25), (-0.3, 45.2), (-11.3, 2.7))
    cells(ax, sq, cmap="gray", vmin=0, vmax=1, text=False, title="Image: white square", lw=0.4, tfs=15)
    arrow(ax, 10.2, -5, 11.3, -5)
    if stage >= 1:
        cells(ax, mv, x=11.6, cmap="Blues", vmin=0, vmax=5, fs=11, fmt=lambda v: n(v) if v else "", title="Layer 1: vertical edges", lw=0.4, tfs=15)
    if stage >= 2:
        cells(ax, mh, x=22.9, cmap="Oranges", vmin=0, vmax=5, fs=11, fmt=lambda v: n(v) if v else "", title="Layer 1: horizontal edges", lw=0.4, tfs=15)
    if stage >= 3:
        arrow(ax, 33.1, -5, 34.5, -5)
        cells(ax, corner, x=34.8, cmap="Greens", vmin=0, vmax=1.6, fs=11, fmt=lambda v: n(v) if v else "", title="Layer 2: corner", lw=0.4, tfs=15)
    return fig


stack([corner_fig(0), corner_fig(1), corner_fig(2), corner_fig(3)])
```
:::

-   Layer 1 has 2 filters, so its output is a stack of two maps, $10 \times 10 \times 2$. ReLU keeps positive responses only, so each map marks one side of the square.
-   A layer 2 filter looks **through the stack**. Take a $1 \times 1 \times 2$ filter with weights $1, 1$ and bias $-3$: $\ z = v + h - 3$.
-   At the top-left corner of the square, $z = 2 + 2 - 3 = 1$. Everywhere else, $z \le 0$, so ReLU gives 0. Only the corner fires.

::: {.key}
**This is hierarchy.** Layer 2 never sees pixels. It sees "edge here" signals, and it combines them into "corner here." Layer 3 can combine corners into shapes, and so on.
:::

## Real Learned Filters: ResNet-18

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{python}
W1 = R["resnet_conv1"]
assert W1.shape == (64, 3, 7, 7)
lim = np.abs(W1).max()
fig, axes = plt.subplots(8, 8, figsize=(6.0, 6.0))
for a, w in zip(axes.ravel(), W1):
    a.imshow((w.transpose(1, 2, 0) / lim + 1) / 2, interpolation="nearest")
    a.axis("off")
fig.subplots_adjust(0.005, 0.005, 0.995, 0.995, 0.06, 0.06)
show_fig(fig)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
-   These are the **64 first-layer filters** of a ResNet-18, a real network trained on 1.2 million ImageNet photos. They are not retouched.
-   Each is $7 \times 7 \times 3$. We can draw it as a tiny color picture because its three channels are red, green and blue.
-   Nobody programmed them. Training found **edges at many angles**, **stripes** and **color contrasts**.
-   Experts had been designing filters much like these by hand for decades. It is a striking result that gradient descent arrives at similar shapes from random numbers.
:::
::::

::: {.key}
Gray means a weight near 0. The first layer has $7 \times 7 \times 3 \times 64 = 9{,}408$ weights (this layer has no bias). The full network has about 11.7 million parameters.
:::

## Through the Layers: Real Feature Maps

```{python}
stage_names = ["conv1", "layer1", "layer2", "layer3", "layer4"]
shapes = {s: tuple(int(v) for v in R[f"stage_{s}_shape"]) for s in stage_names}
assert shapes["conv1"] == (64, 112, 112) and shapes["layer1"] == (64, 56, 56) and shapes["layer2"] == (128, 28, 28) and shapes["layer3"] == (256, 14, 14) and shapes["layer4"] == (512, 7, 7)
assert int(R["resnet_params"]) == 11689512
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(13.4, 4.1))
gs = fig.add_gridspec(2, 11, width_ratios=[2.2] + [1] * 10, left=0.005, right=0.995, top=0.82, bottom=0.03, wspace=0.05, hspace=0.05)
a = fig.add_subplot(gs[:, 0])
a.imshow(R["resnet_photo"])
a.axis("off")
a.set_title("224 × 224 × 3", fontsize=13.5, fontweight="bold", color="#444444")
for j, s in enumerate(stage_names):
    maps = R[f"stage_{s}_maps"]
    for i in range(4):
        a = fig.add_subplot(gs[i // 2, 1 + 2 * j + i % 2])
        a.imshow(maps[i], cmap="magma", interpolation="nearest")
        a.axis("off")
    c_, h_, w_ = shapes[s]
    left = gs[0, 1 + 2 * j].get_position(fig).x0
    right = gs[0, 2 + 2 * j].get_position(fig).x1
    fig.text((left + right) / 2, 0.86, f"{h_} × {w_} × {c_}", ha="center", fontsize=13.5, fontweight="bold", color="#444444")
show_fig(fig)
```

Left to right: a photo passing through a real ResNet-18. Each group shows the 4 most active feature maps at that stage, drawn at the same size so you can see the pixels get coarser.

-   **Height and width shrink:** 224, 112, 56, 28, 14, 7. The network keeps less detail about *where*.
-   **Depth grows:** 3, 64, 64, 128, 256, 512. It keeps more detail about *what*.
-   Early maps still look like the photo. By the last stage, each of the $7 \times 7$ cells summarizes a large area of it.

## True 3D Convolution: Video and Medical Scans

::: {.h360}
```{python}
assert conv_params(3, 3, 1) == 28 and (3 * 3 * 3 * 1 + 1) == 28 and (3 * 3 * 3 * 1 + 1) * 16 == 448
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13.2, 3.4))
for ax in axes:
    ax.set_xlim(-0.6, 18.0)
    ax.set_ylim(-1.7, 8.2)
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.axis("off")
ax = axes[0]
for i, (fc, ec) in reversed(list(enumerate([("#ffd9d6", RED), ("#d6f2dd", GREEN), ("#d9e4ff", BLUE)]))):
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((i * 0.6, i * 0.45), 6, 6, fc=fc, ec=ec, lw=1.4, zorder=3 - i))
block(ax, 1, 3, 3, 3, 2, fc=ORANGE, ec="#a8551c", z=6, ox=0.6, oy=0.45)
arrow(ax, 5.1, 4.5, 7.2, 4.5, color=INK, lw=2.4, z=9)
arrow(ax, 2.5, 2.7, 2.5, 0.6, color=INK, lw=2.4, z=9)
arrow(ax, 8.9, 3, 10.7, 3)
ax.add_patch(Rectangle((11.4, 1), 4, 4, fc=FILL["hid"], ec=ORANGE, lw=1.6))
ax.text(13.4, 5.55, "2D map", ha="center", fontsize=14, fontweight="bold", color="#444444")
ax.set_title("2D convolution on a color image", fontsize=14.5, fontweight="bold", color="#444444")
ax.text(8.2, -1.05, "filter covers the full depth: moves across, down", ha="center", fontsize=13.5)
ax = axes[1]
for i in range(6, -1, -1):
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((i * 0.6, i * 0.45), 5, 5, fc="#eeeeee", ec="#777777", lw=1.0, zorder=8 - i))
block(ax, 2.0, 2.0, 2.2, 2.2, 3.0, fc=ORANGE, ec="#a8551c", z=9, ox=0.6, oy=0.45)
arrow(ax, 6.5, 4.0, 8.1, 4.0, color=INK, lw=2.4, z=11)
arrow(ax, 3.0, 1.8, 3.0, 0.5, color=INK, lw=2.4, z=11)
arrow(ax, 4.9, 5.7, 6.1, 6.6, color=INK, lw=2.4, z=11)
arrow(ax, 9.3, 3, 10.9, 3)
block(ax, 11.4, 1, 3.6, 3.6, 4.0, fc=FILL["hid"], ec=ORANGE, ox=0.6, oy=0.45)
ax.text(14.2, 6.6, "3D map", ha="center", fontsize=14, fontweight="bold", color="#444444")
ax.set_title("3D convolution on a scan", fontsize=14.5, fontweight="bold", color="#444444")
ax.text(8.2, -1.05, "filter is shorter than the depth: moves across, down, through", ha="center", fontsize=13.5)
fig.tight_layout()
show_fig(fig)
```
:::

-   Slices of a CT scan, or frames of a video, are related like neighboring pixels. An abnormal growth spans several slices, and a moving ball changes across frames, so we want the filter to **slide through the third direction too**.
-   Each input slice can also have channels $C$, such as 3 for color video. **Parameters:** $(f \times f \times f \times C + 1) \times k$. For example, 16 filters of size $3 \times 3 \times 3$ on a one-channel scan: $(27 + 1) \times 16 = 448$.

::: {.key}
The same 27 weights can work in two different ways. **What differs is how the filter moves**: a 2D convolution gives a 2D map per filter, and a 3D convolution gives a 3D map per filter.
:::

## The Name Counts Directions, Not Data Dimensions

| Layer | Filter slides along | Typical input | One filter's output | Example filter shape |
|:---:|:-----:|:---------:|:----:|:----:|
| **1D convolution** | time | Audio, sensor readings: $T \times C$ | a 1D list | $5 \times C$ |
| **2D convolution** | height, width | Images: $H \times W \times C$ | a 2D map | $3 \times 3 \times C$ |
| **3D convolution** | height, width, and depth or time | Video, CT and MRI scans: $T \times H \times W \times C$ | a 3D map | $3 \times 3 \times 3 \times C$ |

-   In every row the filter also spans all $C$ channels, and every row uses the same two steps: multiply-and-add, then activation.
-   So a color photo uses a **2D** convolution, though both the image and the filter are 3D arrays. This trips up many people.
-   3D convolutions cost more: for a video, the amount of arithmetic grows with the number of frames too. That is one reason 2D is by far the more common.

::: {.key}
**The path from 2D to 3D:** start with one filter on one grid. Add channels and the filter gains depth. Stack many filters and the output gains depth. Slide through a third direction and you have a true 3D convolution.
:::

# Part 4. A Whole CNN

## Typical Layers in a CNN

**Feature finder:** repeat this block several times. Height and width shrink, and the number of channels grows.

| Layer | What it does | Weights? |
|:--|:--|:--:|
| **Convolution** | Slides $k$ filters over the input and makes $k$ feature maps | Yes: $(f \times f \times C + 1) \times k$ |
| **Batch normalization** | Rescales each channel to mean about 0 and SD about 1 during training, so deep networks train faster and more stably | Yes: 2 per channel |
| **ReLU** | Sets negative values to 0: the nonlinearity | No |
| **Pooling** (max or average) | Shrinks height and width, usually by half | No |

**Decision maker:** turn the final stack into a prediction.

| Layer | What it does | Weights? |
|:--|:--|:--:|
| **Flatten** *or* **global average pooling** | Flatten lines up every number; global average pooling averages each channel to one number, so $7 \times 7 \times 512$ becomes just $512$ | No |
| **Fully connected** | The layers we already know | Yes, often most of them |
| **Dropout** | During training, randomly turns off nodes to fight overfitting | No |
| **Output + softmax** | One node per class, giving probabilities | Yes |

::: {.key}
The common recipe: **[Conv → BatchNorm → ReLU] × a few → Pool**, repeated, then **Flatten or Global Average Pooling → Fully connected → Softmax**. Deep modern CNNs such as ResNet also add **skip connections**, which add a block's input back to its output.
:::

## A Complete CNN, Start to Finish

::: {.h400}
```{python}
assert out_size(28, 3, 1) == 28 and 7 * 7 * 32 == 1568
fig, ax = canvas((13.4, 4.15), (-0.5, 40.5), (-3.6, 9.4))
s_ = 0.14
items = [(0.0, 28, 1, "Input\n28 × 28 × 1", "in"), (6.3, 28, 16, "28 × 28 × 16", "hid"), (13.3, 14, 16, "14 × 14 × 16", "hid"),
         (18.9, 14, 32, "14 × 14 × 32", "hid"), (25.9, 7, 32, "7 × 7 × 32", "hid")]
color = {"in": ("#dfe8ff", BLUE), "hid": ("#FDE3C8", ORANGE)}
for x, wh, d, label, kind in items:
    side = wh * s_
    block(ax, x, 1.6 - side / 2, side, side, d * 0.17 + 0.25, fc=color[kind][0], ec=color[kind][1])
    ax.text(x + side / 2 + 0.7, -1.9, label, ha="center", va="top", fontsize=13.5, color=INK, linespacing=1.25)
ops = [(5.0, "conv 3 × 3\n16 filters\nReLU"), (12.4, "max pool\n2 × 2"), (17.8, "conv 3 × 3\n32 filters\nReLU"), (24.8, "max pool\n2 × 2"), (31.2, "flatten")]
for x, t in ops:
    arrow(ax, x - 0.6, 1.6, x + 0.6, 1.6, color=INK, lw=2)
    ax.plot([x, x], [1.9, 5.0], color="#bbbbbb", lw=1, ls=":", zorder=1)
    ax.text(x, 5.05, t, ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=12.5, color="#444444", linespacing=1.2, zorder=8)
for i, y in enumerate(np.linspace(5, -1.4, 7)):
    if i == 3:
        ax.text(33.1, y, "⋮", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=16)
        continue
    ax.add_patch(plt.Circle((33.1, y), 0.42, fc=FILL["hid"], ec=ORANGE, lw=1.3, zorder=3))
    for y2 in np.linspace(3.7, -0.1, 4):
        ax.plot([33.1, 37.1], [y, y2], color="#cccccc", lw=0.6, zorder=1)
for y2 in np.linspace(3.7, -0.1, 4):
    ax.add_patch(plt.Circle((37.1, y2), 0.42, fc=FILL["out"], ec=GREEN, lw=1.3, zorder=3))
ax.text(33.1, -1.9, "1,568", ha="center", va="top", fontsize=13.5)
ax.text(37.5, -1.9, "10 outputs\nsoftmax", ha="center", va="top", fontsize=13.5, linespacing=1.25)
ax.text(15.0, 8.6, "Part 1: finds features", ha="center", fontsize=15, fontweight="bold", color=ORANGE)
ax.plot([0, 30], [8.2, 8.2], color=ORANGE, lw=2.5)
ax.text(35.3, 8.6, "Part 2: decides", ha="center", fontsize=15, fontweight="bold", color=GREEN)
ax.plot([32.3, 38.4], [8.2, 8.2], color=GREEN, lw=2.5)
show_fig(fig)
```
:::

-   **Feature finder:** repeat convolution, ReLU and pooling. The image gets smaller and the stack gets deeper.
-   **Decision maker:** flatten the final stack, then use the fully connected layers we already know. The output has one node per class, with **softmax** to give probabilities.

::: {.key}
A CNN is a learned feature maker attached to a familiar classifier. The last layer here is multi-class logistic regression, applied to features the network built for itself.
:::

## Trace the Shapes and Count the Parameters

```{python}
pc = [conv_params(3, 1, 16), conv_params(3, 16, 32), fc_params(1568, 10)]
assert pc == [160, 4640, 15690] and sum(pc) == int(R["cnn_params"]) == 20490 and int(R["fc_params"]) == 101770
table(["Layer", "Output shape", "How we get the shape", "Parameters", "How we get the parameters"], [
    ["Input", r"$28 \times 28 \times 1$", "", "0", "Data, not weights"],
    ["Conv, 16 filters", r"$28 \times 28 \times 16$", r"$(28 - 3 + 2) / 1 + 1 = 28$", c(pc[0]), r"$(3 \times 3 \times 1 + 1) \times 16$"],
    ["Max pool", r"$14 \times 14 \times 16$", "Half the height and width", "0", "No weights"],
    ["Conv, 32 filters", r"$14 \times 14 \times 32$", r"$(14 - 3 + 2) / 1 + 1 = 14$", c(pc[1]), r"$(3 \times 3 \times 16 + 1) \times 32$"],
    ["Max pool", r"$7 \times 7 \times 32$", "Half the height and width", "0", "No weights"],
    ["Flatten", "1,568", r"$7 \times 7 \times 32$", "0", "Only rearranges"],
    ["Output", "10", "One node per digit", c(pc[2]), r"$(1568 + 1) \times 10$"],
    ["**Total**", "", "", f"**{c(sum(pc))}**", ""],
])
```

-   Three of the seven layers have parameters. ReLU and pooling add none.
-   Our 784, 128, 10 fully connected network has **101,770** parameters, about 5 times as many.
-   Three quarters of this CNN's parameters ($15{,}690$ of $20{,}490$) are in the single fully connected layer. Convolution is cheap; fully connected layers are not.

## Training: Nothing New

-   **Step 1: the model.** $\hat{y} = f(x, w)$ is the CNN, and $w$ is every filter weight and bias.
-   **Step 2: the loss.** Softmax gives a probability for each class. With $K$ classes, we use **cross-entropy**, the multi-class version of our classification loss:

$$\hat{y}_j = \frac{e^{z_j}}{\sum_{k=1}^{K} e^{z_k}}, \qquad l(\hat{y}, y) = -\log\left(\hat{y}_{\text{true class}}\right)$$

-   **Step 3: find $w$.** Gradient descent, with the gradient computed by backpropagation.

```{python}
ex = -np.log(0.9), -np.log(0.1)
md(f"**Example.** If the model gives the true digit probability 0.9, the loss is $-\\log(0.9) = {ex[0]:.3f}$. If it gives probability 0.1, the loss is $-\\log(0.1) = {ex[1]:.3f}$. Being wrong and confident costs far more.")
```

::: {.key}
**One new detail:** a shared weight is used at every position in the image, so its gradient adds up the contributions from all those positions. Every position in every training image helps train the same filter.
:::

## The Same CNN in Python

```python
import torch.nn as nn

class CNN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.features = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(in_channels=1, out_channels=16, kernel_size=3, padding=1),   # 28 x 28 x 16,  160 parameters
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.MaxPool2d(2),                                                       # 14 x 14 x 16
            nn.Conv2d(in_channels=16, out_channels=32, kernel_size=3, padding=1),  # 14 x 14 x 32,  4,640 parameters
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.MaxPool2d(2),                                                       #  7 x  7 x 32
        )
        self.classifier = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Flatten(),                                                          # 1,568 values
            nn.Linear(1568, 10),                                                   # 10 outputs, 15,690 parameters
        )

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.classifier(self.features(x))
```

-   `Conv2d` is named for its **2 sliding directions**. `in_channels` is the depth $C$ of the input; for color images it would be 3. `out_channels` is $k$, the number of filters.
-   The softmax is built into PyTorch's loss function, `nn.CrossEntropyLoss`. For video or scans, use `Conv3d`. You will build a CNN like this in the assignment.

# Part 5. Why It Works So Well on Images

## Four Reasons, and a Test of Each

| The fact about images | How the CNN uses it | What it gives us | We test it by... |
|:-------------:|:------------:|:----------:|:----------:|
| Nearby pixels are related | Local filters | Fewer parameters | **Experiment 1:** comparing accuracy and size |
| Patterns repeat everywhere | Shared weights | One filter gets trained by the whole image, so less data is needed | **Experiment 2:** using small training sets |
| Objects can be anywhere | Sliding filters and pooling | Some tolerance to shifts | **Experiment 3:** moving the test digits |
| All of the above | The whole design | Good only if the facts are true | **Experiment 4:** breaking the facts |

```{python}
acc = {m: R[f"{m}_by_size"].mean(axis=0) for m in ("fc", "cnn")}
sizes = [int(v) for v in R["sizes"]]
```

**The setup:** real MNIST digits, trained on up to 60,000 images and tested on 10,000 others. Both networks have the same number of gradient descent steps, and every result is an average over 5 random starts.

```{python}
table(["Model", "Layers", "Parameters"], [
    ["Fully connected", "784, 128, 10", c(R["fc_params"])],
    ["CNN", "The network from Part 4", c(R["cnn_params"])],
])
```

```{python}
   f"-   **Size:** it also uses about **{int(R['fc_params']) / int(R['cnn_params']):.1f} times as many** parameters.")
```

::: {.key}
Usually, fewer parameters means a less flexible model. Here the CNN has fewer **and** does better, because its parameters are spent on the kinds of patterns images actually contain.

:::
::::

::: {.key}
Weight sharing acts a bit like having more data. Building a true fact about the problem into the model reduces what must be learned from examples.
:::

## Why Moving the Image Is Not a Disaster

::: {.h300}
```{python}
Vd = V_EDGE
md0 = conv(digit, Vd, mode="same")
moved4 = shifted(digit, dx=4)
md1 = conv(moved4, Vd, mode="same")
assert np.allclose(shifted(md0, dx=4)[:, :-1], md1[:, :-1])   # the last column is the image border
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(13.0, 3.45))
for a, m, t, cm in [(ax[0], digit, "Input", "gray"), (ax[1], relu(md0), "Its feature map", "magma"), (ax[2], moved4, "Input, moved 4 pixels", "gray"), (ax[3], relu(md1), "Same map, moved 4 pixels", "magma")]:
    a.imshow(m, cmap=cm)
    a.set_title(t, fontsize=14.5, fontweight="bold", color="#444444")
    a.axis("off")
fig.tight_layout()
show_fig(fig)
```
:::

-   **Convolution is shift-equivariant:** move the input and the feature map moves by the same amount. The pattern is detected, unchanged, in its new position. In symbols, $\text{conv}(\text{shift}(x)) = \text{shift}(\text{conv}(x))$, ignoring the borders. We checked this equality numerically for this image.
-   **Invariance is a different property:** the output does *not* change at all when the input moves. That is what we want for "which digit is this?"
-   Pooling adds a little invariance at each step. The final fully connected layer does not have it: its weights are still tied to positions in the last $7 \times 7$ map.

::: {.key}
So CNNs have **built-in tolerance** of small shifts, but they are not fully immune to shifts. The next experiment measures how much it helps.
:::

```{python}
    ax.annotate(f"{sfc[i]:.0%}", (dist[i], sfc[i] * 100), xytext=(0, -21), textcoords="offset points", ha="center", fontsize=13)
ax.set_xlabel("Pixels moved (up, down, left or right; training images were not moved)", fontsize=13.5)
ax.set_ylabel("Test accuracy (%)", fontsize=13.5)
ax.set_ylim(0, 108)
ax.yaxis.grid(True, color="#eeeeee")
ax.set_axisbelow(True)
```

```{python}
assert (scn > sfc).all() and scn[2] > 0.9 and sfc[2] < 0.85
md(f"-   Move the digits by 2 pixels, a shift you can barely see, and the fully connected network falls to **{sfc[2]:.0%}** while the CNN stays at **{scn[2]:.0%}**.\n"
   f"-   The CNN's tolerance has limits: at 4 pixels it is down to {scn[4]:.0%}. A larger shift moves patterns across the last $7 \\times 7$ map, where weights are tied to position.\n"
   "-   The usual remedy is **data augmentation**: also train on randomly shifted, cropped and flipped copies of the images.")
```

## Experiment 4: Break the Assumption

```{python}
shf, shc = R["fc_shuffled"].mean(), R["cnn_shuffled"].mean()
assert abs(shf - afc) < 0.002 and shc < shf < acn
```

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="38%"}
```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(5.4, 3.75))
for j in range(3):
    ax[0, j].imshow(digits[j + 6], cmap="gray")
    ax[1, j].imshow(digits[j + 6].ravel()[order].reshape(28, 28), cmap="gray")
    ax[0, j].axis("off")
    ax[1, j].axis("off")
fig.subplots_adjust(0.01, 0.01, 0.99, 0.99, 0.05, 0.05)
show_fig(fig)
```
:::

::: {.column width="62%"}
Shuffle the pixels with one fixed random order, in training and test images alike. All the information is still there, but **neighbors are no longer neighbors**.

```{python}
table(["Test accuracy", "Real images", "Shuffled pixels"], [
    ["Fully connected", f"{afc:.2%}", f"{shf:.2%}"],
    ["CNN", f"{acn:.2%}", f"**{shc:.2%}**"],
])
md(f"-   The fully connected network barely notices, as predicted in Part 1.\n"
   f"-   The CNN loses its lead: it goes from {(1 - acn) * 10000:,.0f} mistakes to **{(1 - shc) * 10000:,.0f}**, about {(1 - shc) / (1 - acn):.1f} times as many, and falls behind the fully connected network. It still works, but its advantage is gone.")
```
:::
::::

::: {.key}
**This is the whole story.** CNNs have no general magic. They win because their assumptions match images. Break the match and the advantage disappears.
:::

This is also why trees and boosting remain strong on **spreadsheets**: rearranging a table's columns changes nothing, so columns have no "neighbors" for a filter to use.

## Depth Lets a Small Filter See a Large Area

::: {.h360}
```{python}
def receptive(layers):
    """layers: (filter size, stride). Grows by (f - 1) x (product of the earlier strides)."""
    r, j = 1, 1
    for f, s_ in layers:
        r += (f - 1) * j
        j *= s_
    return r


assert [receptive([(3, 1)] * t) for t in (1, 2, 3)] == [3, 5, 7]
assert receptive([(3, 1), (2, 2), (3, 1)]) == 8 and receptive([(3, 1), (2, 2), (3, 1), (2, 2)]) == 10
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(9.3, 3.6))
for a, t, col in zip(axes, [1, 2, 3], [GREEN, BLUE, ORANGE]):
    a.set_xlim(-0.1, 9.1)
    a.set_ylim(-0.1, 9.1)
    a.set_aspect("equal")
    a.axis("off")
    for i in range(9):
        for k in range(9):
            a.add_patch(Rectangle((i, k), 1, 1, fc="white", ec="#d0d0d0", lw=0.8))
    side = 1 + 2 * t
    st = (9 - side) / 2
    a.add_patch(Rectangle((st, st), side, side, fc=col, alpha=0.25, ec=col, lw=2.8))
    a.add_patch(Rectangle((4, 4), 1, 1, fc=INK, ec=INK))
    a.set_title(f"{t} conv layer{'s' if t > 1 else ''}: sees {side} × {side}", fontsize=14, fontweight="bold", color="#444444")
fig.tight_layout()
show_fig(fig)
```
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="54%"}
-   The **receptive field** of a node is the patch of the *original image* that can affect it.
-   Each $3 \times 3$ layer adds 2 pixels to its width. Pooling doubles the speed of growth after it.
-   In our CNN: 3, then 4 after pooling, 8 after the next convolution, 10 after the last pooling. Deep networks can reach the entire image.
:::

::: {.column width="46%"}
-   **Why stack small filters?** Two $3 \times 3$ layers see the same $5 \times 5$ area as one $5 \times 5$ layer.
-   They need $9 + 9 = 18$ weights, not $25$ (for one channel in and out), and they add a second ReLU.
-   VGG built a whole network on this idea in 2014.
:::
::::

## A Biological Parallel, and Some Limits

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.view}
Inspired by vision
:::

Hubel and Wiesel studied the visual cortex of cats (1959, 1962; Nobel Prize 1981):

| Brain | CNN |
|:---------:|:-------:|
| **Simple cells:** respond to an edge at one place and angle | Filters |
| **Complex cells:** respond to that edge over nearby places | Pooling |
| Each neuron responds to a small area | Local filters |
| Later areas respond to more complex shapes | Deeper layers |

The link is an analogy, not a model of the brain. For example, the brain does not share weights.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.view}
What a CNN does not get for free
:::

-   **Rotation and scale:** a filter trained on upright edges does not automatically handle rotated objects or objects at other sizes. Data augmentation helps.
-   **The surrounding context:** a small filter sees little, so long-range relations need many layers.
-   **Texture bias:** ImageNet-trained CNNs often lean on texture over shape.
-   **Adversarial examples:** tiny, carefully chosen pixel changes can flip a prediction.
-   **Labeled data:** large models still need many examples, or transfer learning.
:::
::::

# Part 6. How CNNs Changed the Field

## Before and After: Who Designs the Features?

```{python}
def pipe(ax, y, boxes, title, tcol):
    ax.text(0.1, y + 1.5, title, ha="left", va="center", fontsize=15.5, fontweight="bold", color=tcol)
    x = 0.1
    for i, (txt, w, fc, ec) in enumerate(boxes):
        ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((x, y - 0.75), w, 1.5, boxstyle="round,pad=0.02,rounding_size=0.14", fc=fc, ec=ec, lw=1.8, zorder=2))
        ax.text(x + w / 2, y, txt, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=13.5, linespacing=1.25, zorder=3)
        if i < len(boxes) - 1:
            arrow(ax, x + w + 0.08, y, x + w + 0.72, y, color=INK, lw=1.8)
        x += w + 0.8


fig, ax = canvas((13.2, 3.9), (0, 22.2), (-3.4, 3.2))
LG, LO, LB = ("#eeeeee", GREY), ("#FDE3C8", ORANGE), ("#dfe8ff", BLUE)
pipe(ax, 1.05, [("Image", 2.4, *LG), ("Hand-designed features\nSIFT, HOG, color histograms\n(chosen by experts)", 7.2, *LO), ("Trained classifier\nsuch as an SVM", 4.6, *LB), ("Label", 2.4, *LG)], "Before 2012: only the last step learns", ORANGE)
pipe(ax, -2.25, [("Image", 2.4, *LG), ("CNN: feature layers and classifier, all trained together on the same loss", 12.6, *LB), ("Label", 2.4, *LG)], "After 2012: every step learns", BLUE)
show_fig(fig)
```

-   Before: researchers spent careers on better features, and each new task could need new ones. Features for faces did not help with X-rays.
-   After: one recipe works across tasks. Collect labeled data, choose an architecture, train. The question moved from "which features?" to "which architecture and what data?"

::: {.key}
**The real revolution is end-to-end learning.** It is the same shift we saw in the deep learning deck: companies replaced years of hand-built systems once learning won.
:::

## 2012: The Moment Everything Changed

```{python}
years = ["2010", "2011", "2012\nAlexNet", "2013", "2014\nGoogLeNet", "2015\nResNet", "2016", "2017", "Human\n(one test)"]
err = [28.2, 25.8, 15.3, 11.7, 6.7, 3.57, 2.99, 2.25, 5.1]

ax.bar(years, err, color=colors, width=0.62)
for x, v in enumerate(err):
    ax.text(x, v + 0.6, f"{v:g}%", ha="center", fontsize=13, color=INK)
for x, txt in [(2, "8 layers"), (4, "22 layers"), (5, "152 layers")]:
    ax.text(x, err[x] + 3.1, txt, ha="center", fontsize=12.5, color=BLUE, fontweight="bold")
ax.set_ylabel("Top-5 error, winning entry")
```

-   In 2012 the runner-up, using hand-designed features, had **26.2%** error. AlexNet, a CNN, had **15.3%**. Yearly gains had been a couple of points; this was more than ten.
-   Grey bars used hand-designed features. Every winner from 2012 on was a CNN.

## AlexNet, Layer by Layer

```{python}
alex_conv = [conv_params(11, 3, 64), conv_params(5, 64, 192), conv_params(3, 192, 384), conv_params(3, 384, 256), conv_params(3, 256, 256)]
alex_fc = [fc_params(6 * 6 * 256, 4096), fc_params(4096, 4096), fc_params(4096, 1000)]
assert sum(alex_conv) == 2469696 and sum(alex_fc) == 58631144 and sum(alex_conv) + sum(alex_fc) == 61100840
```

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
```{python}
rows = [[f"Conv {i + 1}", s_, c(p)] for i, (s_, p) in enumerate(zip(["64 filters, 11 × 11 × 3", "192 filters, 5 × 5 × 64", "384 filters, 3 × 3 × 192", "256 filters, 3 × 3 × 384", "256 filters, 3 × 3 × 256"], alex_conv))]
rows += [[f"Fully conn. {i + 6}", s_, c(p)] for i, (s_, p) in enumerate(zip(["9,216 → 4,096", "4,096 → 4,096", "4,096 → 1,000 classes"], alex_fc))]
rows += [["**Total**", "", f"**{c(sum(alex_conv) + sum(alex_fc))}**"]]
table(["Layer", "Size", "Parameters"], rows)
```

::: {.note}
Counts are for the standard torchvision version (61.1 million), checked with our rule. The original paper used 96 and 256 filters in its first two layers, split across two GPUs, for about 60 million.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
-   **Same ideas as LeNet-5 from 1998,** far larger: about 1,000 times the parameters.
-   **What was new or newly affordable:**
    -   **ReLU:** in the paper's test, training reached a target error about 6 times faster than with tanh
    -   **Dropout** to reduce overfitting
    -   **Data augmentation:** crops and flips of the images
    -   **Two gaming GPUs:** 5 to 6 days of training
```{python}
md(f"-   **Where the parameters are:** the 5 conv layers have {c(sum(alex_conv))}. The 3 fully connected layers have {c(sum(alex_fc))}, or **{sum(alex_fc) / (sum(alex_conv) + sum(alex_fc)):.0%}** of the total.")
```
:::
::::

::: {.key}
The convolution layers do the seeing with 4% of the parameters. Later networks removed most of that fully connected weight, which is how ResNet-50 got to be far deeper yet smaller: 25.6 million parameters.
:::

## Going Deeper: The Problem and the Fix

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}
fig, ax = canvas((7.8, 4.5), (-1.5, 13.2), (-1.6, 6.5))
ax.text(-0.3, 2.1, "$x$", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=23)
arrow(ax, 0.2, 2.1, 1.2, 2.1, lw=2)
for x, t in [(1.3, "conv\nReLU"), (5.0, "conv")]:
    ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((x, 1.15), 2.6, 1.9, boxstyle="round,pad=0.02,rounding_size=0.15", fc=FILL["hid"], ec=ORANGE, lw=2, zorder=2))
    ax.text(x + 1.3, 2.1, t, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=15, linespacing=1.25, zorder=3)
arrow(ax, 3.95, 2.1, 4.95, 2.1, lw=2)
arrow(ax, 7.65, 2.1, 8.55, 2.1, lw=2)
ax.add_patch(plt.Circle((9.0, 2.1), 0.42, fc="white", ec=INK, lw=2, zorder=3))
ax.text(9.0, 2.1, "+", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=23, zorder=4)
arrow(ax, 9.45, 2.1, 10.45, 2.1, lw=2)
ax.text(11.5, 2.1, "$x + F(x)$", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=20)
ax.plot([0.7, 0.7, 9.0], [2.1, 4.9, 4.9], color=BLUE, lw=2.6)
arrow(ax, 9.0, 4.9, 9.0, 2.55, color=BLUE, lw=2.6)
ax.text(4.8, 5.4, "shortcut: $x$ skips ahead unchanged", ha="center", fontsize=15, color=BLUE, fontweight="bold")
ax.text(4.5, 0.45, "$F(x)$: what the layers add", ha="center", fontsize=15, color=ORANGE, fontweight="bold")
show_fig(fig)
```
:::

::: {.column width="46%"}
**The puzzle:** more layers should never hurt, since extra layers could just pass their input along unchanged. In practice, a 56-layer network had **higher training error** than a 20-layer one. It was harder to optimize, and this was not overfitting.

**The fix (ResNet, 2015):** add the input back. The layers only have to learn the *change*, $F(x)$. To do nothing, they just set $F(x) = 0$.

Gradients can also flow straight along the shortcuts.
:::
::::

| Network | Year | Weight layers | Parameters | Main idea |
|:---:|:--:|:--:|:---:|:------:|
| LeNet-5 | 1998 | 5 | about 60,000 | Conv + pool + fully connected |
| AlexNet | 2012 | 8 | 61.1 million | Scale, ReLU, dropout, GPUs |
| VGG-16 | 2014 | 16 | 138.4 million | Only $3 \times 3$ filters |
| ResNet-50 | 2015 | 50 | 25.6 million | Shortcut connections |

## Transfer Learning: Deep Learning for Everyone

::: {.h300}
```{python}
fig, ax = canvas((10.6, 3.0), (-0.1, 20.5), (-1.7, 3.0))
x = 0.2
labels = [("Edges,\ncolors", 3.2), ("Textures,\ncorners", 3.2), ("Parts,\nshapes", 3.2)]
for lab, w in labels:
    ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((x, -1.35), w, 2.7, boxstyle="round,pad=0.02,rounding_size=0.15", fc=FILL["in"], ec=BLUE, lw=1.8))
    ax.text(x + w / 2, 0, lab, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=13.5, linespacing=1.25)
    arrow(ax, x + w + 0.08, 0, x + w + 0.72, 0, color=INK, lw=1.8)
    x += w + 0.8
ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((x, -1.35), 3.3, 2.7, boxstyle="round,pad=0.02,rounding_size=0.15", fc="#f3f3f3", ec=GREY, lw=1.8, ls="--"))
ax.text(x + 1.65, 0, "1,000\nImageNet\nclasses", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=13, color=GREY, linespacing=1.2)
ax.plot([x - 0.05, x + 3.35], [-1.4, 1.4], color=RED, lw=2.5)
x2 = x + 4.2
arrow(ax, x + 3.45, 0, x2 - 0.1, 0, color=INK, lw=1.8)
ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((x2, -1.35), 3.7, 2.7, boxstyle="round,pad=0.02,rounding_size=0.15", fc=FILL["out"], ec=GREEN, lw=2.2))
ax.text(x2 + 1.85, 0, "New last layer:\nyour classes", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=13.5, linespacing=1.25)
ax.text(6.0, 2.15, "Keep: already trained on millions of photos", ha="center", fontsize=14.5, fontweight="bold", color=BLUE)
ax.text(x2 + 1.85, 2.15, "Train only this", ha="center", fontsize=14.5, fontweight="bold", color=GREEN)
show_fig(fig)
```
:::

-   Early layers learn edges and textures, which are useful for almost any image. So download a trained CNN, replace its last layer, and train only that (and perhaps fine-tune the rest).
-   A task that once needed a million labeled images can often work with dozens or hundreds per class, on a laptop.
-   **Example:** Esteva et al. (2017) reached dermatologist-level skin cancer classification by retraining a network that had first learned from ImageNet.

::: {.key}
This is why CNNs spread so quickly beyond big tech. You will reuse a ResNet-18 on your own images in the assignment.
:::

## CNNs Spread Far Beyond Labeling Photos

| Field | Task | Landmark work |
|:-----:|:----------:|:---------:|
| **Object detection** | Draw a box around each object, in real time | R-CNN (2014), YOLO (2016) |
| **Medical imaging** | Outline structures in scans, pixel by pixel | U-Net (2015) |
| **Medicine** | Detect diabetic eye disease, skin cancer | Gulshan et al. (2016), Esteva et al. (2017) |
| **Games** | Read the Go board as a $19 \times 19$ image with many channels | AlphaGo (2016) |
| **Generating images** | Remove noise step by step, using a U-Net | Stable Diffusion (2022) |
| **Audio** | Treat a spectrogram as an image, or generate raw sound with 1D convolutions | WaveNet (2016) |
| **Video and 3D** | Recognize actions, read CT and MRI volumes | 3D convolutions |

::: {.key}
If you can arrange your data on a grid where neighbors are related, a CNN may work, even if it is not a photo. The Go board is the clearest example: the idea of a local pattern is what mattered.
:::

## The Road So Far

| Year | Event | Why it matters |
|:--:|:----------:|:------------:|
| 1959–1962 | Hubel and Wiesel study the visual cortex | Simple and complex cells: the biological inspiration |
| 1980 | Fukushima's Neocognitron | Stacked local feature layers, but no backpropagation |
| 1989 | LeCun et al. train conv layers with backpropagation | Filters are **learned**, on handwritten zip codes |
| 1998 | LeNet-5 | Commercial system reading several million checks per day |
| 2009 | ImageNet | Enough data to train a large network, and a fair contest |
| 2012 | AlexNet | Won ImageNet by a wide margin: the field switched almost at once |
| 2014–2015 | VGG, GoogLeNet, ResNet | Depth grew from 8 layers to 152, and passed one human's test score |
| 2020 | Vision Transformer | Split the image into patches and use attention: no convolutions |
| 2022 | ConvNeXt | A modernized pure CNN keeps up with Transformer models |

## Where CNNs Stand Today

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.view}
The challenger: Vision Transformers
:::

-   Attention lets any patch relate to any other right from the first layer.
-   They build in **fewer assumptions** about images, so they must learn more from data.
-   Their 2020 paper found they beat CNNs when pre-trained on very large datasets, but fell below comparable ResNets on ImageNet alone without strong regularization.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.view}
The incumbent: CNNs
:::

-   They need less data, thanks to their built-in assumptions, as Experiment 2 showed.
-   They are efficient, so they are a common choice on phones, in cameras, and for real-time work.
-   Well-tuned modern CNNs such as ConvNeXt remain competitive on standard benchmarks.
:::
::::

::: {.key}
This is the **same trade-off** we saw today, and all through the course: build in assumptions and you need less data; if they are limiting, more flexible models can win when data is plentiful. Many modern systems combine both approaches.
:::

## Summary

-   **Problem:** fully connected networks need too many parameters, ignore which pixels are neighbors, and must relearn a pattern at every position.
-   **2D convolution:** a small filter slides across a grid. At each position it does what every node does: multiply, add, activate. Its weights are shared and learned.
-   **To 3D:** channels give the data depth, and the filter depth to match. $k$ filters give an output of depth $k$. Parameters: $(f \times f \times C + 1) \times k$. A true 3D convolution also slides through a third direction, for video and scans.
-   **A whole CNN:** convolution, ReLU, pooling, repeated, then a classifier. Each layer reads the last, moving from edges to parts to objects.
-   **Why it works:** its assumptions (local patterns that can appear anywhere, built up in layers) are true of images. Our experiments show better accuracy with fewer parameters and less data, and they show that the advantage vanishes when we shuffle the pixels.
-   **Why it mattered:** it replaced hand-designed features with end-to-end learning, and transfer learning put that within everyone's reach.

## Problem: A CNN by Hand

```{python}
xp = np.array([[1, 2, 0, 1, 3], [0, 1, 3, 1, 0], [2, 0, 1, 0, 2], [1, 1, 0, 2, 1], [0, 2, 1, 3, 0]])
wp = np.array([[1, 0], [0, -1]])
bp = 1
zp = conv(xp, wp, b=bp)
hp = relu(zp)
pp = pool(hp)
assert zp.shape == (4, 4) and pp.shape == (2, 2)
P = [conv_params(3, 3, 8), conv_params(3, 8, 16), fc_params(8 * 8 * 16, 10)]
assert P == [224, 1168, 10250] and sum(P) == 11642 and out_size(32, 3, 1) == 32
```

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.view}
Part A: one layer
:::

```{python}
fig, ax = canvas((6.8, 3.0), (-0.3, 10.1), (-5.2, 1.0))
cells(ax, xp, face="#f4f4f4", fs=16, title="Image")
cells(ax, wp, x=7.2, y=-1.5, cmap="RdBu", vmin=-2.4, vmax=2.4, fs=17, title="Filter")

ax.text(8.2, -4.2, f"bias $b = {bp}$", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=15)
```

1.  Compute the $4 \times 4$ values of $z$, with stride 1 and no padding.
2.  Apply ReLU.
3.  Apply $2 \times 2$ max pooling.
4.  How many parameters does this filter have?
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.view}
Part B: a whole network
:::

The input is a color image of $32 \times 32 \times 3$. The network has these layers:

-   Conv: 8 filters, $3 \times 3$, padding 1, stride 1, ReLU
-   Max pool: $2 \times 2$
-   Conv: 16 filters, $3 \times 3$, padding 1, stride 1, ReLU
-   Max pool: $2 \times 2$
-   Flatten, then a fully connected output layer with 10 classes

For each layer, find the output shape and the number of parameters. What is the total?
:::
::::

## Problem: Solution

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
::: {.view}
Part A
:::

```{python}
fig, ax = canvas((6.9, 2.5), (-0.3, 13.6), (-4.1, 1.3))
cells(ax, zp, cmap="RdBu", vmin=-6, vmax=6, fs=15, title="$z$", tfs=17)
cells(ax, hp, x=5.1, cmap="Oranges", vmin=0, vmax=7, fs=15, title="ReLU", tfs=15)
cells(ax, pp, x=10.2, y=-1, cmap="Oranges", vmin=0, vmax=7, fs=16, title="Pool", tfs=15)

arrow(ax, 9.25, -2, 10.05, -2)

```

```{python}
md(f"Top-left: $z = {bp} + (1)({xp[0, 0]}) + (0)({xp[0, 1]}) + (0)({xp[1, 0]}) + (-1)({xp[1, 1]}) = {n(zp[0, 0])}$.\n\n"
   f"Next one over: $z = {bp} + (1)({xp[0, 1]}) + (0)({xp[0, 2]}) + (0)({xp[1, 1]}) + (-1)({xp[1, 2]}) = {n(zp[0, 1])}$.\n\n"
   r"**Parameters:** $2 \times 2 \times 1 + 1 = 5$.")
```

::: {.column width="60%"}
::: {.view}
Part B
:::

```{python}
table(["Layer", "Output shape", "Parameters"], [
    ["Conv, 8 filters", r"$32 \times 32 \times 8$", rf"$(3 \times 3 \times 3 + 1) \times 8 = {P[0]}$"],
    ["Max pool", r"$16 \times 16 \times 8$", "0"],
    ["Conv, 16 filters", r"$16 \times 16 \times 16$", rf"$(3 \times 3 \times 8 + 1) \times 16 = {c(P[1])}$".replace(",", "{,}")],
    ["Max pool", r"$8 \times 8 \times 16$", "0"],
    ["Flatten", "1,024", "0"],
    ["Output", "10", r"$(1024 + 1) \times 10 = 10{,}250$"],
    ["**Total**", "", f"**{c(sum(P))}**"],
])
```

Padding 1 with a $3 \times 3$ filter keeps the height and width. The second layer's filter has depth 8 because its input has 8 channels.
